**What it is**

February 2026 Pupil Enrollment Projection Study for the Troy School District, prepared by Plante Moran Realpoint (PMRealpoint), 3000 Town Center, Suite 100, Southfield, MI 48075. Contacts listed are Keith McDonald, Vice President (Keith.McDonald@plantemoran.com, (947) 215-6578) and Paul Wills, Partner (Paul.Wills@plantemoran.com, (248) 223-3316); office (248) 223-3500. Two sections: Section 1 Demographics and Section 2 Pupil Enrollment Projections - Districtwide.

**Section 1 - Demographics**

Charts cover Michigan births and Oakland County births. Oakland County births by birth year, with the kindergarten share of births (K% Birth):

| Birth year | Births | K% Birth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2014 | 13,454 | 6.1% |
| 2015 | 13,547 | 5.3% |
| 2016 | 13,627 | 5.2% |
| 2017 | 13,184 | 5.9% |
| 2018 | 13,152 | 5.3% |
| 2019 | 12,899 | 5.4% |
| 2020 | 12,298 | 5.8% |
| 2021 | 12,877 | 5.5% |
| 2022 | 12,449 | 5.5% |
| 2023 | 12,029 | 5.5% |
| 2024 | 12,233 | 5.5% |
| 2025 | 12,233 | 5.5% |

The 2024 birth counts are provisional and 2025 births are projected. Regionally, 171 out of 233 communities saw a decrease in birth rate between 2002 and 2020. A separate regional analysis forecasts the school-age population (children aged 5 to 17) over the next 30 years, illustrating continued aging of the region, fewer births, migration as a factor in population change, and local trends impacting school districts.

Troy School District population is described as growing and aging, with figures shown for 2010, 2020, 2025 and 2030; the under-18 share is smaller in 2025 than in 2010 while the 65-and-over share has increased. Public versus private enrollment by grade shows the district with a lower public-school share than the county and state for preschool but a higher share for every other cohort, with public share up slightly for each cohort from 2020 to 2025. Household income distribution shifted away from under $100K toward over $100K, particularly the $250,000+ bracket; home values shifted out of the $100K-$400K range and into values greater than $400K.

**Foreign-born population, 2015-2024**

Top countries by percent growth are led by Cameroon (2505%), Croatia (831%), Morocco (686%), Costa Rica (669%), Malaysia (267%), Laos (254%) and the Dominican Republic (243%); Bosnia (80%) ranks 19th. By total population growth, India leads, rising from 5,623 in 2015 to 9,536 in 2024 (24%; 10-year change 3,913), followed by China not including Hong Kong or Taiwan (1,968 to 2,965; 24%; 997), Pakistan (331 to 647; 59%; 316), Mexico (279 to 535; 20%; 256) and Japan (232 to 441; 82%; 209).

**Section 2 - Methodology**

Projections use the Cohort Stability Method, adjusted to community demographic trends, drawing on pupil FTE by grade for the past 7 years and county live birth data by place of residence. Method 1, the most conservative, averages stability percentages from the previous 6 years by grade. Method 2 uses the previous 2 years to exclude outlier years (COVID-19, school of choice changes, new counting methods).

**Section 2 - Districtwide projections**

| Series | 2019 | 2025 | 2030 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All pupils K-12 total | 12,513.46 | 11,411.11 | 10,489.73 |
| All pupils total enrollment | 13,080.61 | 12,043.60 | 11,071.70 |
| Resident only K-12 total | 11,440.20 | 10,727.85 | 10,150.28 |
| Resident only total enrollment | 11,972.62 | 11,337.60 | 10,736.40 |

Projection notes state that resident-only K-12 enrollment declined by 6.2% over the last 7 years while all-pupil enrollment declined by 8.8% over the same period.

The corresponding K% Birth values are 6.1%, 5.3%, 5.2%, 5.9%, 5.3%, 5.4%, 5.8%, 5.5%, 5.5%, 5.5%, 5.5% and 5.5%.

**Section 1: Demographics - regional context**

The overview states that while the region is witnessing the trends of an aging population and reduced birth rates, patterns differ among individual communities and school districts, and that nearly three quarters of communities - 171 out of 233 - in the region saw a decrease in birth rate between 2002 and 2020. Map legends categorize communities as an increase in birth rate 2002-2020, 0 to 1 point decrease, 1.1 to 2 point decrease, 2.1 to 3 point decrease, and more than 3-point decrease. A companion in-depth analysis of forecasted changes in the region's school-age population (children aged 5 to 17) covers the next 30 years and illustrates the continued aging of the region, fewer births, migration as a factor in population change, and local trends impacting school districts; its map legend bands are more than 1,000 loss, 501 to 1,000 loss, 1 to 500 loss, 2 to 500 gain, and more than 500 gain.

**Section 1: Troy School District population, income, and housing**

Total population for the Troy School District is charted for 2010, 2020, 2025 and 2030, with the narrative stating there are more people living in the district in 2025 than were in 2020 and that the district is projected to grow its population slightly through 2030. The population-by-age distribution uses the categories Under Age 5, Age 5-18, 18 & Under, Age 18-29, Age 30-39, Age 40-49, Age 50-64, and Age 65 & Over; the population under the age of 18 represents a smaller share of the total population in 2025 compared to 2010 while the share over the age of 65 has increased significantly, and both trends are projected to continue through 2030. The summary sentence is that the population in the district is growing and aging.

School enrollment trends compare public versus private enrollment by grade for the district, Oakland County and the state: within the district, public schools have a lower share of students than private when compared to the county and state for preschool, but a higher share for every other cohort, and public school enrollment share has increased slightly for each cohort for the district from 2020 to 2025.

Households by income are charted for 2020, 2025 and 2030 using the brackets under $25,000; $25,000-$49,999; $50,000-$74,999; $75,000-$99,999; $100,000-$149,999; $150,000-$199,999; $200,000-$249,999; and $250,000+. The share of households making less than $100K has decreased while the share with incomes greater than $100K has increased, a trend projected to continue into 2030 particularly for the highest bracket of $250K+. Owner-occupied housing units by value are charted for the same three years using the brackets under $50,000; $50,000-$99,999; $100,000-$199,999; $200,000-$299,999; $300,000-$399,999; $400,000-$499,999; $500,000-$749,999; $750,000-$999,999; and $1,000,000+. The share of homes worth $100K-$400K has decreased significantly while the share worth more than $400K has increased significantly, with the trend projected to continue through 2030.

**Section 1: Foreign-born population trends**

Two Census-derived tables cover the Troy School District for 2015-2024. The first ranks countries by percent growth, comparing the average population 2015-2020 to the average population 2020-2024. Cameroon leads at 2505% (10-year change of 99), followed by Croatia 831% (57), Morocco 686% (8), Costa Rica 669% (92), Malaysia 267% (23), Laos 254% (0), Dominican Republic 243% (0), Nepal 189% (76), Indonesia 187% (1), North Macedonia 185% (37), Haiti 158% (7), Ethiopia 146% (-7), France 140% (103), Turkey 126% (68), Uganda 114% (0), Nigeria 100% (48), Australia 100% (24), Japan 82% (209) and Bosnia 80% (53). The narrative notes Cameroon has seen the largest growth in foreign-born population living within the district and Bosnia saw the 19th most growth in 2020-2025 relative to 2015-2020.

The second table ranks countries by total population growth from 2015 to 2024. India rises from 5,623 to 9,536 (24%, 10-year change 3,913); China not including Hong Kong or Taiwan from 1,968 to 2,965 (24%, 997); Pakistan from 331 to 647 (59%, 316); Mexico from 279 to 535 (20%, 256); Japan from 232 to 441 (82%, 209); Canada from 696 to 814 (-1%, 118); France from 8 to 111 (140%, 103); Cameroon to 99 (2505%, 99); Costa Rica to 92 (669%, 92); Cambodia to 91 (0%, 91); Egypt from 275 to 363 (20%, 88); Nepal to 76 (189%, 76); Honduras to 74 (79%, 74); United Arab Emirates to 72 (0%, 72); Bulgaria from 46 to 116 (78%, 70); Turkey from 14 to 82 (126%, 68); Iran from 47 to 109 (7%, 62); Croatia from 9 to 66 (831%, 57); and Bosnia from 36 to 89 (80%, 53). India is described as having by far the largest growth, with Bosnia again 19th.

**Section 2: Methodology**

The projection workflow moves from community demographics, community trends, historical enrollment and live births through a GIS and demographic source and a school district trend from GIS, establishing a baseline, comparing baseline to trend and adjusting, producing a first pass and second pass enrollment projection, then review, verify and confirm before the final Pupil Enrollment Projection Report. Inputs are pupil FTE by grade for the past 7 years and county live birth data by place of residence, with the projection based on the Cohort Stability Method. Method 1, described as the most conservative approach, is based on 6 years of historical data and uses the average stability percentages from the previous 6 years by grade. Method 2 uses the enrollment data by grade of the previous 2 years to determine an assumed stability percentage, allowing exclusion of outlier years arising from internal or external changes or events such as COVID-19, school of choice changes, or new ways of counting students.

Both resident-only and all-pupil enrollment are projected to decline over the next 5 years. Mrs. Anne was elected president, Mrs. Alic vice president, Mr. Haupt secretary and Dr. Melton treasurer, each until December 31, 2026, and the Board awarded gym renovation bids totaling $702,014.00 and elementary toilet room renovation bids totaling $1,377,323.00. The only divided vote was the resolution to opt in to Section 31aa school safety and mental health funds, adopted 6-1 with Mrs. Alic opposed.

**Meeting**

Troy Board of Education Organizational & Regular Meeting, Tuesday, January 20, 2026, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present alongside Dr. Philippart were Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Potts and Zendler, plus Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Yancy, Burden, House and Trudel. About 30 audience members attended. Adjournment was at 8:36 p.m.

**Officer elections (all until December 31, 2026)**

| Office | Elected | Nominated by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acting Chairperson | Nancy Philippart | moved Zendler, supported Alic |
| President | Mrs. Anne | Mrs. Alic |
| Vice President | Mrs. Alic | Mrs. Anne |
| Secretary | Mr. Haupt | Mrs. Alic |
| Treasurer | Dr. Melton | Mrs. Zendler |

Judy Holmes was appointed temporary secretary; nomination closures passed 7-0 and every election carried by roll call, all yes.

**Annual designations**

The fund depositories and investment resolution for January through December 2026 names Bank of America, Citizens Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank) and PNC Bank; investments follow Board Policy 5000.06 and Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code. Legal counsel for calendar 2026: Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Miller Canfield. The Superintendent continues as Deputy Secretary, Judy Holmes is designated to post meeting notices, and the 2026 meeting schedule and Board Committee Memberships were adopted. All 7-0.

**Recognition, consent agenda, personnel (7-0 each)**

January is School Board Appreciation Month. The TSD Mission Moment honored the Superintendent Student Advisory Board Executive Committee, which leads the 56-member SSAB and ran the MLK Citywide Celebration and Day of Service: Nicholas Dilis, Vihaan Gehlaut, Everett Marshall, Ridhi Maruneni, Angelina Matti and Errikos Perakis. Consent agenda items A-E covered minutes of the December 9, 2025 Workshop and December 16, 2025 Board Meeting; Treasurer Report - November 2025; Budget Amendment #1; and the Secondary Course Description Book. The Troy Educational Secretaries Association (TESA), MEA/NEA and Troy Educational Support Personnel Association (TESPA), MEA/NEA contracts were both extended through June 30, 2030. Curriculum: none.

**Business awards (Capital Projects Fund and Building Site and Sinking Fund)**

AHS & THS Main and Aux Gym Remodel: Zak Welding & Custom Work, misc iron, $39,600.00; RNC Paint Systems, painting, $15,000.00; Floor Care Concepts, gym flooring, $67,314.00; Interkal LLC, bleachers, $528,363.00; Trist Creek Flooring, Inc., flooring, $12,000.00. Subtotal $662,277.00, contingency (6%) $39,737.00, total $702,014.00.

Elementary Toilet Room Renovations: Great Lakes Construction, demolition, $143,440.00; Culver Development, concrete, $48,000.00; Seven Brothers Painting, Inc, painting, $43,650.00; Continental Interiors, flooring, $93,315.00; Omega Floors, hard tile, $149,500.00; Mid Thumb Contracting, general trades, $312,424.00; CSM Mechanical, mechanical, $306,970.00; Max Electric LLC, electrical, $178,000.00. Subtotal $1,275,299.00, contingency (8%) $102,024.00, total $1,377,323.00.

**Section 31aa opt-in**

The State School Aid Act for 2025-2026 was signed into law October 7, 2025; Section 31aa allocates $321,000,000.00 statewide and requires districts to opt in, agree to a comprehensive investigation, and waive privilege in the event of a mass casualty event. A Michigan Court of Claims order of November 21, 2025 allowed districts opting in by 11:59 p.m. December 4, 2025 to rescind by 11:59 p.m. December 30, 2025. The Board believes the waiver requirement is likely unconstitutional but wants the school safety and mental health funds; the waiver is limited to a mass casualty event occurring after receipt of funds through the end of the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Adopted 6 yes (Anne, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, Zendler) to 1 no (Alic).

**Closing**

One community member spoke on agenda items and five on non-agenda items. Student representatives Bella Doss (Troy High School), Sara Graunstadt (Athens High School), Ahyoung Song (International Academy-East) and Chloe Gentilini (Troy College and Career High School) reported. The next Board Workshop was set for Tuesday, February 3rd and, due to mid-winter break, the next regular meeting for Tuesday, February 24th.

Approximately 30 members of the audience attended. Dr. Philippart explained that the evening's meeting is where the Board selects officers, appoints committee members, approves the meeting schedule, and authorizes annual items, with the regular meeting following under the newly elected president. The Pledge of Allegiance followed.

**Organizational actions**

Election of Acting Chairperson: moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Alic that Nancy Philippart serve as Acting Chairperson to preside over the Organizational Meeting until completed; Yes 7, No 0. Dr. Philippart appointed Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until the secretary of the Troy Board of Education was elected.

President: Mrs. Alic nominated Mrs. Anne; nominations closed on a motion by Mr. Haupt supported by Mrs. Anne, Yes 7, No 0; moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that Mrs. Anne serve as president until December 31, 2026, with roll call recording Anne, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, Zendler and Alic all voting yes. Vice President: Mrs. Anne nominated Mrs. Alic; nominations closed on a motion by Mrs. Potts supported by Mrs. Anne, Yes 7, No 0; moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that Mrs. Alic serve until December 31, 2026; roll call all yes. Secretary: Mrs. Alic nominated Mr. Haupt; nominations closed on a motion by Mrs. Anne supported by Mrs. Alic, Yes 7, No 0; moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that Mr. Haupt serve until December 31, 2026; roll call all yes. Treasurer: Mrs. Zendler nominated Dr. Melton; nominations closed on a motion by Mrs. Alic supported by Mr. Haupt, Yes 7, No 0; moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Anne that Dr. Melton serve until December 31, 2026; roll call all yes. The minutes text for the treasurer item repeats the word secretary in the nomination and resolution wording.

**Fund depositories and investment resolution**

Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board adopt the resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments for the period January through December 2026, incorporated in its entirety into the official minutes; Yes 7, No 0. Michigan law requires the Board to provide by resolution for the deposit of all public monies, including tax monies, coming into the hands of the Treasurer of Troy School District; the resolution directs deposit and/or investment into Bank of America, Citizens Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), and PNC Bank. Monies may be withdrawn by checks signed with a facsimile signature of the Treasurer, and in emergencies the handwritten signature of the Treasurer, the Assistant Superintendent of Business, or the Superintendent, who may sign on the General Fund account and the Payroll account at Bank of America. Accounts established at PNC Bank for paying Troy Career Center expenses may be withdrawn by checks with the handwritten signature of the Troy Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager, or Program Coordinators. The Treasurer or Assistant Superintendent of Business may open or close accounts when in the District's interest; funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06; and money from more than one fund may be combined for an investment authorized by subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code, with the maximum amount to be invested regulated by the school code. Matt Haupt, Secretary of Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, certified adoption on the 20th day of January 2026.

**Other annual designations**

Designation of Board and District Legal Counsel, moved by Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic, continued Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Miller Canfield as legal counsel for the 2026 calendar year, with the superintendent authorized to consult additional counsel as needed with prior notification to the board; Yes 7, No 0. Designation of the Superintendent of Schools as Deputy Secretary of the Board for 2026, moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mr. Haupt; Yes 7, No 0. Designation of Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools, as the person for posting notices of meetings for 2026, moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Zendler; Yes 7, No 0. Adoption of the 2026 meeting schedule, moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic; Yes 7, No 0. Adoption of Board Committee Memberships for 2026, moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt; Yes 7, No 0.

**Recognitions**

Board Recognition Month: each January the Troy School District honors the trustees of its Board of Education, recognizing their role in shaping policies, fiscal stewardship, and support of world-class teaching and learning under the district mission of ensuring learning for all. TSD Mission Moment: the Board recognized the Superintendent Student Advisory Board Executive Committee, which leads the 56-member SSAB by planning, setting agendas, running meetings, and orchestrating activities and events, and which organized and executed the MLK Citywide Celebration and Day of Service attended by hundreds of families. The six executive board members recognized were Nicholas Dilis, Vihaan Gehlaut, Everett Marshall, Ridhi Maruneni, Angelina Matti and Errikos Perakis. A five minute recess followed. Yes 7, No 0.

**Resolution to Opt-In to Receive Section 31aa Funds**

The State School Aid Act for the 2025-2026 school year was signed into law on October 7, 2025, and Section 31aa allocates a total of $321,000,000.00 to all districts throughout the state, with districts required to opt in to be eligible. To receive funding, a district, intermediate district, nonpublic school, or the Michigan Schools for the Deaf and Blind must agree to be subject to a comprehensive investigation, must affirmatively agree to waive any privilege that may otherwise protect information from disclosure in the event of a mass casualty event, and must comply with the investigation. The investigation assesses emergency response effectiveness, compliance with safety protocols, communication procedures, and contributing factors; the governor designates the investigator, which may include state law enforcement agencies, independent review boards, or specially appointed task forces, with authority to access records and data, interview witnesses and district personnel, and issue findings. A detailed report goes to the governor and relevant legislative committees within 90 days following the conclusion of the investigation. A mass casualty event is defined as an incident on school grounds or at a school-sponsored event resulting in significant injuries to not fewer than 3 individuals, resulting in fatalities, exceeding the normal resources for emergency response available in the jurisdiction, or resulting in a sudden and timely surge of injured individuals necessitating emergency services. An order of the Michigan Court of Claims entered on November 21, 2025 provides that a district opting in by 11:59 p.m. on December 4, 2025 may subsequently rescind that decision by 11:59 p.m. on December 30, 2025. The Board believes the waiver requirement is likely unconstitutional and would be an intolerable burden on its ability to operate, but desires the funds for school safety and mental health programs and recognizes that the Superintendent already conditionally opted in; the Superintendent is further authorized to execute future 31aa documents as required by MDE. Any waiver is limited to a mass casualty event occurring after the District receives the funds, through the end of the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Board members shared reluctance due to vague language and legislation requiring districts to waive their rights, conflicting with federal privacy laws protecting students and employees from waiving attorney-client privilege. Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Potts; Yes 6 - Anne, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, Zendler; No 1 - Alic. Certified by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Board of Education, Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, with notice given under the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267, as amended.

**Identification**
Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education, Tuesday, May 19, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The record is filed as M051926BdMtg within the June 16, 2026 board packet. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. and it was adjourned at 8:27 p.m. Minutes were respectfully submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary of the Troy Board of Education, with typist initials MH/jh.

**Attendance**
In addition to Mrs. Anne, board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts and Zendler were present. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Keegan, Cottone, Wallace, Cronin, Griffin, Hall, Montante, Pagel and Trudel. Approximately 125 members of the audience attended. The meeting opened with the Pledge of Allegiance.

**Recognition: Outstanding Support Staff**
The board presented the Outstanding Support Person of the Year award, a category covering bus drivers, secretaries, paraprofessionals, student support aides, custodial staff, food service, technology, childcare, security and more. There were 25 nominees. The 2026 honoree is Matt Snitgen, a paraprofessional at Athens High School in the MOCI Room, nominated by Rebecca Roy. The nomination praised his unwavering belief in his students, noting that he sees potential where others often see limitations, and cited his positivity, compassion and work ethic. It described how he models and encourages communication in all forms, including body language, gestures, facial expressions and AAC devices, treating every communicative attempt as meaningful. A student was quoted saying, "We have a secret handshake. Mr. S is a great person because he's nice and he makes me feel happy and excited to be at school." Snitgen's name was engraved on the Support Person Plaque, to be displayed at his building for the next year, and a short video of the surprise visit was shown.

**Legislative CAP Students Report**
Students from the Legislative track of the Career Accelerator Program (CAP) reported on their engagement with the school board, the city, and state senators and representatives. Troy Center for Transition teacher Brynn Lawrence and International Academy East teacher Mark Chrzanowski were invited to the podium to introduce their students. **Schools of Character Recognition**
Hamilton Elementary School and Troy Union Elementary School were honored as National Schools of Character, two of just 72 schools nationwide to receive the distinction from Character.org. Schroeder Elementary School, Troy Union Elementary School and Boulan Park Middle School were named State Schools of Character, and Wattles Elementary School and Barnard Elementary School received Honorable Mention. Character.org also recognized Troy Union and Wattles as the only schools in Michigan to earn recognition for Promising Practices, highlighting innovative efforts that strengthen school culture, encourage student leadership and service, and promote goodness in action.

Teacher Appreciation Week was celebrated Monday, May 4 through Friday, May 8, 2026. It resolved that the Troy School District supports National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 4-8, 2026. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Mental Health Awareness Month resolution**
Introduced with reference to Oakland Community Health Network and its service provider network and to other school boards across Oakland County. Moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Dr. Philippart, the resolution recited that one in five of all Americans, including children, experience mental health issues that could lead to school difficulties, physical problems and even suicide; that May 7, 2026 is designated National Children's Mental Health Awareness Day; and that May 3 through May 9, 2026 is designated Children's Mental Health Acceptance Week. It resolved that the Troy Board of Education recognizes May 2026 as Mental Health Awareness Month. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

One community member addressed the board. No action was taken by the board.

**Other: Oakland Schools Biennial Election**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Haupt. The resolution recited that Mich. Comp. Laws section 380.614 requires a constituent school board to designate its representative and identify the Intermediate School Board candidate it supports by a resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days prior to the election; that the statute prescribes consideration of the resolution at not less than one public meeting before adoption; and that the board previously considered the resolution at an open meeting conducted under the Open Meetings Act on May 19, 2026. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Troy School District administration update to the Board of Education on middle school mathematics, presenting March 2026 survey feedback on the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum and the middle school course progression adopted in May 2023. Survey participation totaled 2,059 students (72 percent of the population), 398 parents and guardians (14 percent), and 21 staff (81 percent). The staff results were markedly critical: 11 of 21 math teachers (52.4 percent) called for revisiting or revising the math progression model, and the most-cited curriculum theme was insufficient materials and practice problems, named by 12 respondents (57.1 percent). Administration said it would bring a recommendation to the Board at the April 28 workshop.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Purpose**
Middle school math update presenting survey feedback gathered in March 2026 on instructional practices in math classrooms, implementation of Illustrative Mathematics (IM), student learning, and middle school course progression. Presented to the Troy Board of Education for the April 7, 2026 meeting.

**Historical context**
The prior curriculum, Big Ideas, was described as outdated and not aligned to the district's vision for math. The Board of Education adopted the new curriculum and new progression in May 2023. Administration committed to annual review of student achievement data (M-STEP/PSAT), annual review of course enrollment data (Honors Algebra 1), annual collection of staff, student and family feedback, implementation of NWEA, ongoing teacher support, and continued building of MTSS structures. Board commitments were to review annual data sets and understand the implementation timeline, described as a 3-5 year implementation, with a note that adoption does not require a 7 year cycle if other concerns arise.

**Achievement data reviewed**
M-STEP results have been reviewed annually for grades 6 and 7: grade 6 in 2024 (first year of implementation data), grade 6 in 2025 (second year), and grade 7 in 2025 (first year). For the 8th grade PSAT in 2026 no achievement data is available yet; that cohort is the first with full implementation of the new program. The n values printed with the achievement charts are (567), (607), (643), (576), (642) and (677).

**Honors enrollment**
Under '8th Grade Enrollment Trends in Honors Math Courses (Algebra 1 and Above)', the presentation states the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in student enrollment in honors and that the district will continue to monitor. Total students shown across the periods charted: (907), (961), (995), (1023).

**Survey participation**

| Survey group | Participation count | Percentage of total population participating |
|---|---|---|
| Student Survey | 2,059 | 72% |
| Parent/Guardian Survey | 398 | 14% |
| Staff Survey | 21 | 81% |

**Staff survey results (n=21)**

| Response | Count | Percent |
|---|---|---|
| Most students understand the goals of the lessons because the work is at the right level | 7 | 33.3% |
| Most students feel lost even after asking questions or reviewing material | 7 | 33.3% |
| Most students are underchallenged and would like more advanced work | 1 | 4.8% |
| Understand goals + underchallenged | 2 | 9.5% |
| Underchallenged + feel lost | 2 | 9.5% |
| All three responses | 2 | 9.5% |

**Themes needing attention**
Within the progression model: too much content in Honors Algebra 1 combined with Math 8 (7, 33.3%); difficulty with differentiation covering pacing, learning gaps and student supports (5, 23.8%); underchallenged students (5, 23.8%); fear of lower outcomes for Algebra 1 students (4, 19.0%). Within the IM curriculum: insufficient materials/practice problems (12, 57.1%); not enough scaffolding or differentiation (8, 38.1%); pacing too fast (7, 33.3%); concerns about Algebra 1 content combined with Math 8 (7, 33.3%); too much focus on story problems (4, 19.0%); negative CoTeach AI experience (4, 19.0%).

**Teacher view of the progression**
Revisit/revise the model 11 (52.4%); no opinion stated 8 (38.1%); favorable view 1 (4.8%); mixed view 1 (4.8%).

**Next steps**
Free response data from parents and students will be coded and analyzed. Administration will prepare a recommendation for the Board at the 4/28 workshop, anticipated to cover supplemental resources, convening a curriculum review team including middle school math teachers, and exploring accelerated pathways, with formal board consideration in winter/spring 2027 for implementation in fall of 2027.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Identification.** 'MS Math Update Survey Feedback March 2026', a Troy School District administration presentation to the Board of Education carried in the April 7, 2026 packet (file titled MS Math Update BOE 4.6.26).

**Historical context.** The presentation opens by noting outdated math materials and that the former curriculum, Big Ideas, did not align to the district's vision for math. The Board of Education adopted the new curriculum and the new progression in May 2023.

**Commitments made at adoption.** TSD Administration committed to: annual review of student achievement data (MSTEP/PSAT); annual review of student course enrollment data (Honors Alg 1); annual collection of feedback from staff, students and families; implementation of NWEA; investment in ongoing teacher support; and continuing to build MTSS structures to support student growth. The TSD Board of Education committed to review annual data sets, to understand the implementation timeline of the new curriculum, described as a 3-5 year implementation timeline, and noted that adoption does not require a 7 year cycle if other concerns arise.

**Curriculum adoption and implementation cycle.** A four-part cycle is depicted: Explore, Research and Vision, Implementation, and Curriculum Review Cycle. Under Research and Vision the district researches best instructional practices, reviews state standards, ensures alignment with the TSD strategic plan, and examines district data trends to identify needs; it compiles and proposes a list of potential resources for early-adopter and pilot teams; assembles a content area curriculum review team of teachers and administrators as suggested by math leadership teams; and creates partnerships with experts, learning organizations and local school districts. Under Explore the district narrows potential resources with curriculum review teams, explores multiple resources with students through a pilot and/or early-adopter experience, gathers qualitative and quantitative student and teacher data on engagement, student performance, joy and usability, and supports pilot and early-adopter classrooms through professional learning, district-wide collaboration, classroom visits, out-of-district site visits, coaching, and learning beyond the school day. Under Implementation the district implements the new curriculum as recommended by the curriculum review and math leadership teams and seeks School Board approval, supports implementation through professional learning, job-embedded coaching, classroom visits and district-wide collaboration, continues professional learning with in-district, local and national partnerships, and reviews qualitative and quantitative data and adjusts.

**Academic achievement data.** The district has annually reviewed M-STEP data for 6th and 7th grade. The data points listed are: MSTEP 6th grade 2024 (first year of implementation data); MSTEP 6th grade 2025 (second year of 6th grade implementation data); MSTEP 7th grade 2025 (first year of implementation data); and PSAT 8th grade 2026, for which no academic achievement data is available yet, that 8th grade being the first cohort to have full implementation of the new program. The n values printed beneath the achievement charts are (567), (607), (643), (576), (642) and (677).

**8th grade honors enrollment.** A section titled '8th Grade Enrollment Trends in Honors Math Courses (Algebra 1 and Above)' summarizes that the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in student enrollment in honors and that the district will continue to monitor middle school honors math enrollments. The total students figures shown across the four charted periods are (907), (961), (995) and (1023).

**Survey purpose and participation.** The district administered a survey to middle school students, parents/guardians, and math teachers to gather feedback on instructional practices within math classrooms, curriculum implementation of Illustrative Mathematics, student learning, and course progression for middle school math. Participation was: Student Survey 2,059 participants, 72 percent of the total population; Parent/Guardian Survey 398 participants, 14 percent; Staff Survey 21 participants, 81 percent.

**Student and parent response options.** The full text of the survey response choices reported for the student math experience question were: 'I usually understand the goals of the lesson because the work is at the right level for me'; 'I feel underchallenged by lessons and I would like more opportunities for advanced work'; and 'I feel lost even after asking questions or reviewing material'.

**Staff survey responses (n=21).** Seven respondents (33.3 percent) said most students understand the goals of the lessons because the work is at the right level for them. Seven respondents (33.3 percent) said most students feel lost even after asking questions or reviewing material. One respondent (4.8 percent) said most students are underchallenged by lessons and would like more opportunities for advanced work. Two respondents (9.5 percent) selected both the 'understand the goals' and 'underchallenged' statements. Two respondents (9.5 percent) selected both 'underchallenged' and 'feel lost'. Two respondents (9.5 percent) selected all three statements.

**Identified areas of improvement, math progression model.** Main themes needing to be addressed within the current math progression model: too much content in Honors Algebra 1 combined with Math 8, 7 responses, 33.3 percent; difficulty with differentiation covering pacing, learning gaps and student supports, 5 responses, 23.8 percent; underchallenged students, 5 responses, 23.8 percent; fear of lower outcomes for Algebra 1 students, 4 responses, 19.0 percent.

**Identified areas of improvement, IM curriculum.** Main themes needing to be addressed within the current IM curriculum: insufficient materials, specifically practice problems, 12 responses, 57.1 percent; not enough scaffolding/differentiation within the curriculum, 8 responses, 38.1 percent; curriculum pacing too fast, 7 responses, 33.3 percent; concerns about Algebra 1 content combined with Math 8, described as lower rigor and too much content, 7 responses, 33.3 percent; too much focus on story problems, 4 responses, 19.0 percent; negative CoTeach AI experience, 4 responses, 19.0 percent.

**Math teacher perspective on the current math progression.** Revisit/revise the math progression model, 11 responses, 52.4 percent; no opinion stated, 8 responses, 38.1 percent; favorable view of the math progression model, 1 response, 4.8 percent; mixed view of the math progression model, 1 response, 4.8 percent.

**Pending analysis.** The presentation states that in the coming weeks free response survey data from both parents and students will be coded and analyzed to inform next step decision making.

**AI summary.** A slide labeled 'AI Summary (CoPilot)' reproduces the prompt used: attached are survey results from math teachers on current math curriculum and math course progression, provide a summary of the survey responses. The executive summary produced states that the survey reveals significant concerns among math teachers about both the IM curriculum and the current course progression model, particularly around pacing, differentiation, foundational skill gaps, and Algebra 1 in 8th grade; that while some teachers value the instructional philosophy and student discourse supported by IM, the prevailing tone is negative to mixed, with widespread calls for more balance, clearer pathways, and stronger supports. Overall takeaways listed: IM philosophy has merit but materials are insufficient on their own; foundational skills and fluency require far more emphasis; differentiation is difficult without structural changes to courses or curriculum; Algebra 1 in 8th grade is a critical pain point affecting students, teachers, and outcomes; and teachers want clear learning targets, flexible pacing, and defined pathways rather than scripted constraints.

**Next steps.** Administration asked for additional time to review feedback, collaborate with the team, and prepare a recommendation to the Board at the 4/28 workshop. Anticipated topics in the recommendation, based on teacher survey feedback, are: adoption of supplemental resources to support student learning in response to staff, student, and family feedback; convening a curriculum review team inclusive of middle school math teachers; and exploring accelerated pathways for middle school students and accompanying curriculum. The process would include board consideration and adoption of a formal recommendation in winter/spring 2027 for implementation in fall of 2027.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A 21-slide Troy School District secondary mathematics presentation on the Geometry and Honors Geometry program review and curricular adoption, brought to the Board of Education as item 3D. It reports on two years of piloting, in which OpenUp Mathematics was piloted for Quarter 1 of 2024-25 and discontinued on teacher feedback while Illustrative Mathematics was piloted for Quarters 2, 3 and 4 and then across all of 2025-26, with 100 percent of Geometry teachers and 88 percent of Honors Geometry teachers participating. The recommendation is adoption of Illustrative Math Geometry with additional fluency practice through DeltaMath and printed student workbooks.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Item and scope**
Secondary Math, Geometry and Honors Geometry: Program Review and Curricular Adoption, a PowerPoint presented to the Troy Board of Education for April 7, 2026 as item 3D.

**Framing**
The deck reviews the eight Standards for Mathematical Practice (make sense of problems and persevere; reason abstractly and quantitatively; construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; model with mathematics; use appropriate tools strategically; attend to precision; look for and make use of structure; look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning) and the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices, citing NCTM (2014), Principals to Actions: Ensuring mathematical success for all. The district vision, citing NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics, holds that all students are doers of mathematics and that the program should cultivate positive mathematical identities so students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics.

**Current status**
The current resource has been in use for over 15 years, creating alignment challenges between teachers and across buildings. Current resources present topics taught in sequence rather than a storyline that builds conceptual understanding over time, and do not explicitly provide tools or strategies to make learning accessible for all students. High school math curriculum options are described as more limited, with everything requiring adjustment and supplementation.

**Pilot process**

| Year | Materials piloted | Teacher participation | Structure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-25 | OpenUp Mathematics and Illustrative Math | 70% of Geometry teachers | OpenUp in Quarter 1, discontinued on teacher feedback about time constraints, lack of teacher guidance and explicit practice; IM in Quarters 2, 3 and 4 |
| 2025-26 | Illustrative Math | 88% of Honors Geometry teachers; 100% of Geometry teachers | IM piloted for the school year |

Both years included monthly cohort meetings with job-embedded professional learning. The Geometry cohort partnered with the Michigan Math and Science Leaders Network (MMSLN), which provided professional learning on teaching IM, supported prioritizing Geometry standards to open room for curriculum aligned to postsecondary pathways in Statistics, Quantitative Reasoning or Data Science and the TSD portrait of a learner, is developing a Data Science module based on Troy teachers' input, and facilitated the monthly cohort meetings.

**Course distinction**
Geometry covers conceptual understanding of proof and conceptual understanding and application of geometry. Honors Geometry adds conceptual understanding and application of proof, algebraic application of geometry, additional and more advanced trigonometry concepts, extensions through projects and additional algebra work, and a faster pace.

**Teacher perception data (15 of 16 geometry teachers)**
Celebrations: 10 out of 15 feel confident using IM and 3 out of 15 somewhat confident; 13 out of 15 feel confident navigating IM resources; 13 out of 15 feel IM moves the district toward a problem-based, student-centered curriculum. Challenges: 13 out of 15 feel they lack adequate sample communications and tools for parents; 12 out of 15 feel tools for struggling learners are insufficient; 10 out of 15 feel extension tools are insufficient.

**Recommendation and supports**
Adopt Illustrative Math Geometry with additional fluency practice and printed student workbooks. Supports include the 2026 Math Summer Institute (3 days prior to back-to-school professional learning), back-to-school PL days, a full day of district professional learning, Math Specialist coaching and intervention, quarterly collaboration meetings for Geometry and monthly for Honors Geometry, DeltaMath subscriptions, and IM Family Support Materials and lesson summaries posted on Schoology.

**Monitoring**
Goals are growth in the number of students scoring advanced or proficient on PSAT and SAT exams and improvement in achievement, problem solving and communication of mathematical thinking measured by internal common assessments; measures reported annually include PSAT/SAT with cohort data and NWEA, with unit and common assessments and student grades in higher levels of mathematics studied with staff.

**Identification.** '3D 2026 Geometry BOE Presentation', a 21-slide PowerPoint titled Secondary Math, Geometry and Honors Geometry: Program Review and Curricular Adoption, presented to the Troy School District Board of Education for the April 7, 2026 meeting.

**Guiding learning and standards.** The deck states the district has engaged in extensive learning as it continues its secondary math review and adoption process. It lists the Standards for Mathematical Practice: make sense of problems and persevere in solving them; reason abstractly and quantitatively; construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; model with mathematics; use appropriate tools strategically; attend to precision; look for and make use of structure; and look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning. It then presents the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices, stating that to ensure mathematical success for all students mathematics education will involve these practices and that they allow teachers to implement the Michigan K-12 Math Standards, citing NCTM (2014), Principals to Actions: Ensuring mathematical success for all.

**Vision.** The Troy School District Mathematics Department believes all students are doers of mathematics and that the purpose of the mathematics program is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. The citation given is NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

**Current status.** The district has used its current resource for over 15 years and has made the curriculum its own, which presents challenges such as alignment between teachers and across buildings. Current resources are topics taught in sequence rather than a storyline that intentionally builds conceptual understanding over time, and do not explicitly provide tools or strategies to support teachers in making learning accessible for all students. The district has collaborated with districts across the county and with national experts, and reports that options for high school math curricula are more limited and that everything requires some adjustments and supplementation.

**Pilot process, 2024-25.** Based on the team's review matrix, the team piloted OpenUp Mathematics and Illustrative Math. Seventy percent of Geometry teachers participated in the pilot. OpenUp was piloted for Quarter 1 and discontinued due to teacher feedback regarding time constraints, lack of teacher guidance, and explicit practice. Illustrative Math was piloted for Quarters 2, 3 and 4 because the team wanted to see the entire story of the year unfold. Professional learning and support consisted of monthly cohort meetings with job-embedded professional learning.

**Pilot process, 2025-26.** The team piloted Illustrative Math. Eighty-eight percent of Honors Geometry teachers participated in the IM pilot and 100 percent of Geometry teachers participated. IM was piloted for the school year. Support again consisted of monthly cohort meetings with job-embedded professional learning, and the Geometry cohort partnered with the Michigan Math and Science Leaders Network.

**MMSLN partnership.** The Michigan Math and Science Leadership Network provided professional learning around teaching the Illustrative Math curriculum; supported the team in prioritizing Geometry standards to create the opportunity for additional curriculum aligned to postsecondary pathways of Statistics, Quantitative Reasoning, or Data Science and to the TSD portrait of a learner; is developing a Data Science module based on Troy teachers' input and direction; and supported facilitation of the monthly meetings with the Geometry cohort.

**IM philosophy and sample items.** Slides assert that IM aligns with the district vision and describe the IM philosophy as problem-based, student-centered teaching and learning. Separate slides display a sample SAT problem and a sample AP exam question.

**Geometry versus Honors Geometry.** Geometry is characterized by conceptual understanding of proof and conceptual understanding and application of geometry. Honors Geometry is characterized by conceptual understanding and application of proof, conceptual understanding and algebraic application of geometry, additional and more advanced trigonometry concepts, extensions in the form of projects and additional work with algebra, and a faster pace.

**Teacher perception data, celebrations (15 of 16 geometry teachers responding).** Ten out of 15 feel confident using IM and 3 out of 15 feel somewhat confident. Thirteen out of 15 feel confident navigating the IM resources. Thirteen out of 15 feel IM moves the district toward its goal of implementing a problem-based, student-centered math curriculum. Two teacher quotations are included: one stating that what the teacher enjoys about the current curriculum is that it encourages students to think about the 'why' behind the math instead of just memorizing steps, with appreciation for the focus on student discussion and multiple ways of approaching problems; and one stating enjoyment that there is a storyline, that students build on previous ideas and use that knowledge to problem solve, and that the curriculum teaches through applications with students often asked to explain their thinking rather than just get to an answer.

**Teacher perception data, challenges.** Thirteen out of 15 feel they do not have adequate sample communications or tools to provide parents with resources for at-home support; the plan is a printed workbook, extra practice with DeltaMath, and IM Lesson Summaries and Family Resources posted on Schoology. Twelve out of 15 feel the tools provided to support struggling learners are not sufficient; the plan is extra practice with DeltaMath, professional learning on Tier 2, UDL, IM routines and formative assessment, and collaboration time. Ten out of 15 feel the tools provided for extension are not sufficient; the plan is extension problems with DeltaMath and collaboration time to develop extension activities.

**Adaptations based on challenges.** A quoted teacher describes being challenged by the lack of resources that come with the curriculum, wanting projects or challenge problems with each section or unit rather than relying on the 'are you ready for more' feature; the plan is regular collaboration time during the school day to create additional resources. A second quoted teacher describes challenges with the accessibility of some lessons, noting that while the curriculum emphasizes conceptual understanding many students still need more structure, clearer examples and more guided practice; the plan is professional learning on the direct instruction moments embedded within IM, plus DeltaMath and CoTeach AI to create more guided and independent practice. The deck states these plans were developed collaboratively with teachers.

**Recommendation.** Illustrative Math Geometry with Additional Fluency Practice and Printed Student Workbooks. The stated rationale: a problem-based curriculum built on a Universal Design for Learning framework; embedded supports for students with disabilities and English Learners; extensions for students who are ready for more; built-in instructional routines that support teachers and students; predictable and purposeful activity and lesson structure; practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review; additional fluency practice using DeltaMath; and printed student workbooks.

**Continued support of implementation.** The 2026 Math Summer Institute consisting of 3 days of learning prior to back-to-school professional learning; back-to-school professional learning days; a full day of learning during district professional learning; Math Specialist support to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach teachers, and do intervention with struggling students; quarterly collaboration meetings including job-embedded learning for Geometry; and monthly collaboration meetings including job-embedded learning for Honors Geometry.

**Support for families.** Every IM unit includes a Family Support Materials section describing in plain language the big ideas students will encounter, providing an overview of the mathematics, details about what to expect as learning deepens, and questions that promote conversation about the mathematics. Every IM lesson includes a lesson summary written to summarize the main mathematical points and any new vocabulary in student-friendly language, intended for students to read on their own time or to catch up after an absence, and useful for families.

**Course materials.** All course resources will be accessed through the IM platform, with additional resources housed in Schoology. Student workbooks will be provided to all students, and student workbooks and family resources will be posted on Schoology. As requested by teachers, DeltaMath subscriptions will be purchased to support additional practice and fluency for classroom use and for work sent home.

**Monitoring success.** Goals are to see growth in the number of students who score advanced or proficient on PSAT and SAT exams, and improvement in student achievement, problem solving skills, and communication of mathematical thinking as monitored through internal common assessment. Measurement may include, reported annually, PSAT/SAT including cohort data and NWEA; and studied with staff, unit assessments and common assessments and student success (grades) in higher levels of mathematics.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Identification**
Draft 2025-26 Troy School District Student Code of Conduct, 16 pages, prepared through Miller Johnson School Policy Services and copyrighted to Miller Johnson for the sole and exclusive use of Miller Johnson and the Troy School District. Presented as item 3C for the April 7, 2026 Board of Education meeting.

**Acknowledgements, athletics, transportation, searches**
Students and parents sign the Acknowledgement of Receipt annually at registration through PowerSchool Forms; a footnote defines 'parents' to include legal guardians. Athletics participation is a privilege, not a right, governed additionally by the TSD Athletic Handbook, acknowledged in Final Forms. Student drivers must be licensed, permitted, registered and parked in designated areas, conditioned on advance consent to vehicle search at any time for any reason. Bus misconduct costing transportation privileges includes insubordination, smoking/vaping, fighting, profane or foul language, and destruction of property. Students have no reasonable expectation of privacy in lockers, desks or assigned technology devices.

**Dress and appearance**
Required: a shirt of opaque fabric with some form of shoulder strap, opaque bottoms, and shoes. Prohibited: violent language or images; drug, alcohol or vaping imagery; body armor or tactical gear; hate speech, profanity, pornography; visible undergarments; swimsuits outside class or practice; dangerous accessories such as handcuffs; and anything obscuring the face except religious observance or PPE. Hats and hooded sweatshirts are allowed if the face stays visible.

**Bullying and cyberbullying**
Each building Principal is primarily responsible for implementing administrative regulation 2006AR and its corresponding policy. The Superintendent reports all verified incidents and consequences to the Board annually. Retaliation is a serious violation of Board Policy 2000.06 independent of substantiation, as are intentionally false reports. Where bullying is alleged to be based on race, color, sex, national origin or disability, the principal notifies the district Compliance Officer or Coordinator under Board Policy 8000.07 and Administrative Regulations 8007AR and 8007.1AR.

**Discipline thresholds**

| Term | Definition in the Code |
|---|---|
| Short-term suspension | 10 school days or fewer |
| Long-term suspension | More than 10 school days; procedurally, 11 school days or more |
| Suspension (definition) | Exclusion for fewer than 60 school days, or until conditions are met |
| Expulsion | Exclusion for 60 school days or more, or permanent exclusion |

Seven factors must be considered and documented before long-term suspension or expulsion: the student's age; disciplinary history; whether the student is disabled within the meaning of IDEA or ADA/Section 504; seriousness of the misconduct; whether it threatened the safety of any pupil or staff member; whether restorative practices will be used; and whether less severe discipline would suffice. The presumption does not apply to short-term suspensions or to a student possessing a firearm in a weapons free school zone. Restorative practices teams may be constituted under Section 1310c(2) of the Revised School Code.

**Attendance**
The Code quotes Revised School Code 380.1561 requiring attendance from age six to the child's eighteenth birthday. Students get one day per excused day to make up work, up to 10 days. Secondary students arriving within five minutes of the start of class are marked tardy and later arrivals get an unexcused tardy, with 3 tardies per class per marking period allowed before detention. A parent must call within 24 hours for an absence to be excused. Long-term absences in excess of 5 days and not to exceed 10 days must be prearranged one week in advance on an Extended Absence form. Email notices go out at the 5, 7 and 9 absence point in any semester; chronic absenteeism brings a staff meeting and referral to the Oakland County Truancy Officer.

**Prohibited acts**
Thirty-six numbered offenses, among them alcohol and marijuana, arson (MCL 750.71 through MCL 750.80), bullying and hazing, criminal sexual conduct (MCL 750.520b-e and g), dangerous weapons including a knife with a blade over 3 inches, drugs, electronic devices and laser pointers, gang insignia, look-a-like weapons, recording without consent, scholastic dishonesty, vaping, acceptable use violations expressly covering artificial intelligence and large language models, and weapons including a knife with a blade length of three inches or less.

**Due process**
A building administrator's suspension of up to ten school days is final and not subject to review or appeal. Suspensions of 11 to 59 days may be appealed in writing to the building principal and Assistant Superintendent within five days. Recommended expulsions require a hearing with the Assistant Superintendent, commencing within ten school days if the student is suspended pending the hearing or scheduled within fifteen school days if not. The decision is given orally within five school days of the close of the hearing with a written decision mailed at the same time; permanent expulsion may be appealed to the Superintendent within five school days, and the Superintendent renders a written decision within fifteen school days.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Identification and copyright.** TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT STUDENT CODE OF CONDUCT, a draft for 2025-26 presented as agenda item 3C in the April 7, 2026 Board of Education packet. The document runs 16 pages and carries a Miller Johnson School Policy Services notice stating it is copyrighted to Miller Johnson, intended for the sole and exclusive use of Miller Johnson and the Troy School District, and that no portion may be reproduced, copied, distributed, or sold without prior written permission.

**Introduction.** The School District must balance the interests of students and the community in a safe and conducive educational environment with its duty to provide educational services to students who engage in misconduct. Board of Education policies and the Code are intended to strike that balance but do not limit the district's lawful authority. All students and parents must sign the Acknowledgement of Receipt of the Student Code of Conduct annually when students are registered for the school year, completed through PowerSchool Forms. A footnote states that 'parents' includes legal guardians and, where required by law, those acting in the place of parents.

**Athletics and transportation.** Participation in interscholastic or extracurricular athletics is a privilege, not a right; student athletes are subject to the Code at all times plus the TSD Athletic Handbook, acknowledged annually by parents and athletes through Final Forms and posted on the TSD Athletics webpage. Student drivers must be licensed and receive district permission to park on district property or use a vehicle during the school day, must register with their school and park only in designated areas, conditioned on advance consent to search of their vehicles at any time, for any reason, with or without notice. Bus riders must obey the driver's direction; misconduct examples that may suspend transportation privileges include insubordination, smoking/vaping, fighting, profane or foul language, and destruction of property.

**Dress and appearance.** Students must wear a shirt with opaque fabric in front, back, and on the sides under the arms plus some form of shoulder strap; bottoms of opaque material including pants/jeans or the equivalent such as skirt, sweatpants, leggings, dress, or shorts; and shoes. Courses that include attire as part of the curriculum, such as professionalism, public speaking, and job readiness, may include assignment-specific dress, and activity- or course-specific shoe requirements are permitted such as athletic shoes for physical education or recess and closed toe shoes for science labs and industrial arts. Prohibited are violent language or images; images or language depicting or suggesting drugs, alcohol, vaping or paraphernalia or any illegal item or activity; body armor, tactical gear, or facsimile; hate speech, profanity, pornography; clothing revealing visible undergarments, though visible waistbands and straps are allowed; swimsuits except as required in class or athletic practice; accessories that could be considered dangerous or used as a weapon such as handcuffs or other metal accessories; and any item that obscures the face except as a religious observance or as personal protective equipment such as medical face masks. Hats, hooded sweatshirts and other head coverings are permitted but must leave the face visible to staff and not interfere with anyone's line of sight.

**Police, search and seizure.** The district cooperates with local police; parents will be notified if police arrest or wish to question their student in school, with timing depending on circumstances, and except as required by law the district retains discretion to report crimes. Students have no reasonable expectation of privacy in school property assigned to them such as lockers, desks and technology devices, and the district reserves the unrestricted right to search and seize such property at any time, for any reason, with or without notice. Illegal or inappropriate items may be confiscated and delivered to police or parents.

**Bullying and cyberbullying.** The Principal of each building is primarily responsible for implementing administrative regulation 2006AR and its corresponding policy. The Superintendent shall report to the Board of Education annually all verified incidents of bullying and the resulting consequences. 'Bullying' means any written, verbal, or physical act, or any electronic communication including cyberbullying, intended or reasonably known to be likely to harm one or more students by substantially interfering with educational opportunities, benefits, or programs; adversely affecting a student's ability to participate in or benefit from educational programs by placing the student in reasonable fear of physical harm or causing substantial emotional distress; having an actual and substantial detrimental effect on physical or mental health; or causing substantial disruption in the orderly operation of the school. 'At school' means in a classroom, anywhere else on school premises, on a school bus or other school-related vehicle, and at a school-sponsored activity or event whether or not on school premises, and includes off-premises use of a telecommunications access device or service provider owned by or under the control of the district. Retaliation against a target, witness, reporter or participant in an investigation is prohibited and is a serious violation of Board Policy 2000.06 independent of whether a complaint is substantiated; intentionally false reports are likewise prohibited. Victims must immediately report to the building principal, assistant principal, or counselor, and the parent must also report; the principal or designee conducts a prompt investigation and may first attempt informal resolution such as restorative practices, with the complainant free to request a formal investigation at any time. Where bullying is alleged to be based in whole or in part on race, color, sex, national origin, or disability, the principal notifies the district's designated Compliance Officer or Coordinator pursuant to Board of Education Policy 8000.07 and Administrative Regulations 8007AR and 8007.1AR.

**Rebuttable presumption and the seven factors.** Consistent with Michigan law the district adopts a rebuttable presumption that students should not be disciplined by long-term suspension, meaning more than 10 school days, or expelled, meaning 60 or more school days, unless the district determines in its sole discretion that the presumption has been rebutted after considering each of seven factors: the student's age; the student's disciplinary history; whether the student is disabled within the meaning of IDEA or ADA/Section 504; the seriousness of the misconduct; whether the misconduct threatened the safety of any pupil or staff member; whether restorative practices will be used; and whether less severe discipline would properly address the misconduct. The presumption does not apply to short-term suspensions of 10 school days or fewer or to a student who possesses a firearm in a weapons free school zone, but the administrator must consider and document the seven factors for all long-term suspensions and expulsions. Restorative practices must be considered in every case as an addition or alternative to suspension or expulsion; a restorative practices team may be constituted and act in the manner described in Section 1310c(2) of the Revised School Code, and restorative practices should be the first consideration for interpersonal conflicts, bullying, verbal and physical conflicts, theft, damage to property, class disruption, and harassment.

**Definitions of discipline.** Administrative intervention is disciplinary action not resulting in suspension and may include removal from a class period, in-school suspension, reprimand, restitution, detention and/or work assignment before or after school, additional classroom assignments, and revocation of the privilege of attending after school functions. Suspension is exclusion from school for fewer than 60 school days or exclusion terminating upon fulfillment of specific conditions. Expulsion is exclusion from the district for 60 school days or more or permanent exclusion.

**Attendance.** The Code quotes the Revised School Code (380.1561) requiring every parent, guardian or other person having control of a child from the age of six to the child's eighteenth birthday to send that child to the public schools during the entire school year. Excused reasons include chronic or serious illness, religious observances, family bereavement, mandatory court appearance, college visits, or other reasons approved by a building administrator. Students receive one day for each day excused absent to make up work, up to 10 days, including tests and quizzes; work assigned before an absence is due on return. School-sponsored activities such as field trips, athletic contests, counselor appointments, student club obligations and school business are exempted absences. Students must sign in or sign out in the designated office when entering or leaving at other times. Elementary schools develop their own truancy procedures, communicated at the beginning of each year. At middle and high school, students arriving within five minutes after the start of class are marked tardy and later arrivals receive an unexcused tardy; students are afforded 3 tardies per class per secondary marking period without penalty, after which detention is assigned. A parent must call the attendance office within 24 hours for an absence to be excused; any absence not excused within 24 hours remains unexcused, and unexcused absences may bar makeup of missed assessments, labs or presentations. Long-term absences in excess of 5 days and not to exceed 10 days must be prearranged and approved one week in advance through an Extended Absence form available in each school's main office. Families receive email communication including class attendance status at the 5, 7 and 9 absence point in any semester, listing the course name, total number of absences, and whether excused or unexcused. Chronic absenteeism results in a meeting with school staff and referral to the Oakland County Truancy Officer and other county resources.

**Range of discipline and jurisdiction.** Penalties range from administrative intervention to expulsion, from suspension to expulsion, or expulsion alone, with the actual penalty depending on the nature and severity of the offense, the facts, the student's age, prior behavioral record, chronic nature of the misconduct, staff recommendation and other relevant circumstances. The Code applies to prohibited acts on school property; in a motor vehicle including one used for a school-related purpose; at a school-related activity, function or event; en route to or from school; involving another student en route to or from school; off school premises where the act is prohibited by law or is serious enough in the building administrator's judgment that continued attendance would endanger health and safety or substantially interfere with the educational process; and acts committed before enrollment in Troy School District or while enrolled elsewhere.

**The 36 prohibited acts.** 1 Alcohol, Marijuana, and Chemical Substances. 2 Arson. 3 Arson Prohibited by Law, citing MCL 750.71 through MCL 750.80 and supplemental to paragraphs 2, 12, 22 and 36. 4 Bullying and Hazing, referencing Board Policy 2000.06 and AR 2006. 5 Coercion, Extortion, and Blackmail. 6 Copyrighted Material. 7 Criminal Acts. 8 Criminal Sexual Conduct as defined by MCL 750.520b-e and g, supplemental to paragraphs 9, 10, 14, 24, 25 and 35. 9 Discriminatory Harassment covering race, color, national origin, religion, sex including sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, marital status, pregnancy status, genetic information, disability or age. 10 Disruption of School. 11 Damage of Property or Theft/Possession. 12 Dangerous Weapons, listing brass knuckles, dagger, dirk, firearm, iron bar, knife with a blade over 3 inches in length, pocket knife opened by a mechanical device, or stiletto. 13 Dress. 14 Drugs, Narcotic Drugs, and Counterfeit Substances. 15 Electronic Communication Devices and Laser Pointers. 16 Failure to Comply with Directions of School Personnel. 17 Failure to Cooperate. 18 False Alarms. 19 False Allegations. 20 Falsification of Records. 21 Fighting, Assault, and Battery on Another Person. 22 Fireworks, Explosives, and Chemical Substances. 23 Gang Insignia/Activity, defining 'gang' as a group of two or more persons whose purpose or activities include illegal acts or Code violations. 24 Improper Communications. 25 Indecency. 26 Look-A-Like Weapons such as a starter pistol, rubber knife or toy gun. 27 Misconduct Prior to Enrollment. 28 Personal Protection Devices such as pepper gas, mace, stun gun or electric shock device. 29 Recording, barring capture or transmission of audio or images of any person at school or school-related events without express consent. 30 Trespassing, Loitering. 31 Scholastic Dishonesty including plagiarism. 32 Smoking/Tobacco/Vaping, including electronic cigarettes and vaporizers. 33 Suspended Student on School Property or Attending School Activities. 34 Violation of Acceptable Use Policy, stating that uses of artificial intelligence, large language models, or similar technology are subject to the Acceptable Use policy and the Code. 35 Violations of Building's Rules and Regulations. 36 Weapons and Dangerous Instruments, covering a knife with a blade length of three (3) inches or less, air soft gun, blackjack, baton, martial arts device, paint ball or splat gun.

**Personal technology guidelines.** Districtwide, students may not use or possess active electronic communication devices in restrooms, locker rooms, offices and other locations with a reasonable expectation of privacy, and laser pointers are barred without express administrative permission. Elementary: phones and personal devices must remain on silent with notifications disabled and stored in backpacks or lockers during school hours, with no one-way or two-way communication during the school day unless approved by a TSD staff member; wearable technology such as Apple Watches and Fitbits is allowed with notifications off and communication features disabled; earbuds or headphones require staff permission. Middle school: personal technology may not be used during the school day and must remain out of sight until the end of the day including passing time and lunch, stored in lockers, though personal cell phones may be used in the main office. High school: phones and personal technology must be stored in a locker or backpack during class time. The district is not responsible for lost, stolen or damaged personal technology; students use district-provided iPads during instruction.

**Due process, short-term suspension.** Before any out-of-school suspension the building administrator will inform the student of the misconduct and, if denied, explain the evidence; allow the student to explain their version of the facts; and consider each of the seven individual factors, including restorative practices. If the student's presence poses an immediate danger or ongoing threat of disruption the administrator may suspend immediately and provide due process as soon thereafter as reasonable. The administrator may impose a suspension not to exceed ten school days, must inform the parent in person or by phone and then in writing, and that decision is final and not subject to further review or appeal.

**Due process, long-term suspension and expulsion.** Step 1: for a suspension of eleven or more school days or expulsion, the student and parent are notified in writing of the charges, the potential range of disciplinary action, the fact that a hearing will be held with the building administrator, and the time, place, location and procedures; that hearing will take place within five days of the disciplinary event to the extent practicable, and the notice documents consideration of the seven factors and of restorative practices. A recommended suspension of 11 to 59 days may be appealed in writing to the building principal and Assistant Superintendent within five days. All recommended expulsions of 60 school days or more, and permanent expulsions, require a hearing with the Assistant Superintendent. If the student is suspended pending the decision the hearing commences within ten school days following the initial suspension after the principal's investigation is complete; if not suspended, it is scheduled within fifteen school days following completion of the investigation, with timelines subject to enlargement on request. Step 2: the Assistant Superintendent hearing determines the truth or falsity of the charges and, if found true, considers the seven factors, restorative practices and appropriate discipline; the student or parent may waive the hearing, in which case the principal's recommended penalty is ordinarily imposed except that expulsion or permanent expulsion remains the Assistant Superintendent's decision; charges may be amended and a greater or lesser penalty imposed. Step 3: the decision is given orally not later than five school days after the close of the hearing, with a written decision mailed at the same time, subject to enlargement for extenuating circumstances. Step 4: a decision to permanently expel may be appealed to the Superintendent by written notice filed with the Assistant Superintendent and Superintendent within five school days; the appeal involves no further testimony or new evidence, the Assistant Superintendent shares the hearing results and a recommendation, the student, parent or legal representative may address the Superintendent, and the Superintendent renders a written decision within fifteen school days. During suspension, expulsion or permanent expulsion a student may not participate in or attend school-sponsored activities on or off campus, nor be on district property.

**Inconsistency clause.** The Code is intended to be consistent with Michigan law, Board of Education policies, and Administrative Regulations promulgated by the Superintendent; inconsistencies are resolved with Michigan law superseding both Board policies and Administrative Regulations, and Board Policy superseding Administrative Regulations.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Statement of Public Necessity and Declaration of Taking of Private Property by which the Troy School District, acting through its Board of Education, moves to condemn permanent highway and sidewalk easements over property at 5836 Livernois Road, Troy, tax parcel 20-10-101-033, owned by Mirza Azam-Ali Baig and Juveria Baig.
