**Instrument and item**
Statement of Public Necessity and Declaration of Taking of Private Property, agenda item 3.B for the April 7, 2026 Troy Board of Education meeting, file reference 287251943.1. It is to be recorded with the Oakland County Register of Deeds and is dated April 2026 with the day left blank.

**Project**
The Troy School District, a Michigan general powers school district acting through its Board of Education, is undertaking construction and operation of the new Smith Middle School on Livernois Road in the City of Troy, Oakland County, which includes roadway and sidewalk improvements for public benefit and to improve road conditions, safety, mobility and accessibility. Property commonly known as 5836 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan, Tax Parcel No. 20-10-101-033, owned in fee by Mirza Azam-Ali Baig and Juveria Baig. A permanent highway easement is depicted in Exhibit 1 and a permanent sidewalk easement in Exhibit 2.

**Property.** Commonly known as 5836 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan; Tax Parcel No. 20-10-101-033. The permanent highway easement is depicted in Exhibit 1 and the permanent sidewalk easement in Exhibit 2, together the Easements, depicted on the attached surveys.

**Individuals or entities believed to have an interest in the Easements.** (1) Mirza Azam-Ali Baig and Juveria Baig, husband and wife, the Owner. (2) The Huntington Bank as Lender, mortgage recorded December 3, 2025, Liber 60771, Page 843, Oakland County Records. (3) City of Troy, sidewalk easement, as set forth in the Declaration of Taking in Oakland County Circuit Court, Case #84-281475 CC, recorded August 1, 1989, Liber 10522 Page 049, Oakland County Records. (4) Oakland County, water supply system easement, as set forth in Oakland County Circuit Court Case #73-105515 CC, recorded February 21, 1974, Liber 6260, Page 334, Oakland County Records.

**Estimated just compensation.** Estimated just compensation for the Highway Easement is $5,662.80. Estimated just compensation for the Sidewalk Easement is $935.00. Estimated total just compensation is $6,597.80.

**Failed negotiations and statutory authority.** The document recites that negotiations with the Owner to acquire the Easement have not been successful. Pursuant to Section 11a of Michigan Public Act 451, Public Acts of 1976, the Revised School Code, as amended, MCL 380.11a, the district has power to acquire interests in real property by condemnation pursuant to the Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act, Public Act 87 of 1980, as amended, MCL 213.51 et seq. The UCPA establishes certain procedures for the taking of property by eminent domain. The district reserves the right to bring federal or state cost recovery actions against the Owner for costs incurred as a result of the release of hazardous or toxic substances or materials which may have occurred on the Easement.

**Superintendent's authority and declaration.** As Superintendent of the Troy School District, the signer states he has authority on behalf of the district as provided by the attached Troy School District Resolution Declaring the Necessity to Acquire Highway and Sidewalk Easements and to authorize Clark Hill PLC to institute condemnation proceedings as to the easements, dated April 7, 2026, to acquire such easements by condemnation. **Property taxes.** Budgeted to rise 3.4%, a conservative figure against Oakland County Equalization's expectation of just over 4.0% growth in county taxable values. **Identification and statutory context.** Oakland Schools' "Original Budget for the fiscal year 2026-27," a combined external budget book printed 03/24/2026, appearing in Troy School District Board of Education materials dated May 19, 2026. Oakland Schools is one of 56 Michigan intermediate school districts established in 1962, an autonomous tax-supported district under Michigan General School Law; its mission statement is "Every Student. Every Day." Cited compliance obligations are the General Property Tax Act (Public Act 206 of 1893, MCL 211.24e), the Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act (Public Act 2 of 1968), and the Revised School Code (Public Act 451 of 1976, MCL 380.624 and MCL 380.684). The ISD board must submit its proposed budget to each constituent district board for review and comment by May 1; adoption follows a public hearing and must occur by June 30 for the year beginning July 1, 2026. Governing policies are 3050 (budget preparation), 3100 (annual operating budget and amendments), 3150 (fund balance) and 3170 (budget transfer authority); amendments come at least three times a year, and Board Policy 3230 requires reporting of cooperative-service subsidies.

**Enterprise-wide totals.** Proposed total funding is $563.2 million: property taxes $270.7 million; other local and investment revenue $51.7 million; state source revenue $24.8 million; other financing sources and indirect revenue $15.8 million; estimated grant award funding $200.2 million. Proposed total expenditures are $591.7 million: salary, wage and benefits $88.8 million; purchased services, supplies, utilities and dues/fees $27.2 million; capital outlay $23.9 million; transfers to LEAs and other funds $233.4 million; grant-related expenditures $200.2 million; payment on existing debt $18.2 million. Both are net of eligible inter-company eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund amounts.

**Revenue assumptions.** Property tax revenue is budgeted up 3.4%, or $9.0 million, a conservative estimate against Oakland County Equalization's projection of just over 4.0% county taxable value growth; taxable values reached pre-recession levels in 2022-23. The tax base is 70% principal residence and 30% non-principal residence, and the District saw a Headlee rollback in ten of the last eleven years. By fund: General Education Fund $15,547,600 to $16,076,200; Special Education Fund $197,835,800 to $204,562,200; Career Focused Education Fund $48,379,700 to $50,024,600; total $261,763,100 to $270,663,000, a change of $8,899,900. The Michigan Tax Tribunal reserve is budgeted at .25% of tax revenues, approximately $676,700. Investment revenue totals $7,893,400 against $8,778,500, most funds down 20.0% while Debt Service Funds rise from $419,000 to $1,206,000. Other local revenue totals $43,764,200 against $42,095,900. State source revenue totals $24,811,800 against $25,599,000; Section 81 ISD Operations rises 2.0%, Section 27L(4) Healthcare Offset one-time funding is removed, and Section 147a(2) MPSERS Normal Cost Offset loses a one-time adjustment. Grant revenue totals $200,249,800 (state $136,389,300, federal $61,993,900, local $1,866,600).

**Personnel and benefits.** Staffing moves from 642.9 to 650.1 FTE, a net 7.2 increase: elimination of a 1.0 FTE Human Resources Manager; a .5 FTE reduction in the Business Office Residency Program, from four residents to three for part of the year; a .3 FTE reduction in District & School Services Pupil Services part-time staff; a new 1.0 FTE Shipping/Receiving Warehouse Supervisor; 6.0 FTE for the new Special Populations Continuum of Supports unit; and 2.0 FTE in Technology Services for Artificial Intelligence. An across-the-board 2.0% increase applies to all staff; the collective bargaining agreement expires June 30, 2027. Non-union step growth is assumed at 1.3% and union wage base growth at .9%. Health care uses the hard cap with 4.0% medical CPI growth: family $21,660.30 to $22,526.71; individual plus one $16,609.38 to $17,273.76; single $7,942.09 to $8,259.77. **Meeting**

The Troy High Boys' Tennis Team was honored. Following runner-up finishes in each of the past two seasons and returning 11 of 12 starters from the 2024 season, the team won a State Championship. **Recognition - Troy High Boys' Tennis Team**
The Board recognized the Troy High Boys' Tennis Team. The narrative notes the team was motivated by runner-up finishes in each of the past two seasons and entered the year determined to represent their city with pride. Returning 11 of 12 starters from the 2024 season, the group consistently demonstrated maturity, discipline, and experience throughout the year. The defining lesson of the season was that yesterday's setbacks can become today's success, a mindset the players embraced from the first day forward, and their commitment was ultimately rewarded with a State Championship. The players recognized and celebrated were Sourish Daruri, Quentin Gatto, Krish Gupta, Jesse Hao, Jonathan Jung, Raghav Karur, Vyom Kashi, Jyotiraditya Kashyap, Derrick Kyung Chan Kim, Solmin Kim, Jackson Kraus, Neel Nagappala, Nikhil Nair, Varun Shetty, Zain Taqi, Nathan Wanstreet, Anthony Wu, and Dheeraj Yelleti.

**Additions and Deletions; Public Communication on Agenda Items**
Both items were recorded as None.

It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Board of Education issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Dr. Jordan Dennis, who will begin his duties as Supervisor, Data and Research effective January 5, 2026. **Curriculum**
Recorded as None.

The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

One community member addressed the Board during public communication. No action was taken by the Board.

**Other - OCSBA Resolution on Non-Partisan School Board Elections**
It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Zendler that the Troy Board of Education approves the proposed new resolution as presented: OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Other - OCSBA Resolution on Full Funding of Early On Michigan**
It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board of Education approves the proposed new resolution as presented: OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays or who are at risk for delays due to certain health conditions. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

Chloe Gentilini, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, shared a report on the events and activities happening in her school. Board members wished everyone a Merry Christmas and Happy Holidays. **Presentation**
Middle School Math Update, Board Workshop - January 2026, Troy School District.

**Vision**
All students are doers of mathematics; the program's purpose is to cultivate positive mathematical identities so that students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. Sourced to NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

**May 2023 Findings**
Finding 1, explore curricular changes: program data from the last 5 years preceding COVID showed performance slightly decreasing or stagnant, with cohort data showing a decrease in students achieving advanced and proficient and an increase in students not proficient. Finding 2, explore course sequencing: students do not fluidly move between tracks in middle school. Finding 3, explore classroom pedagogy: task-based, inquiry-based instruction building procedural fluency through conceptual understanding.

**Recommendation and Course Choice (May 2023)**
The recommendation was Illustrative Math: problem-based, built on Universal Design for Learning, with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners, extensions, built-in instructional routines, and practice sets with cumulative review. Math 8 was framed as the natural transition from Math 7 covering linearity, functions, and geometry; Honors Algebra 1 embeds Math 8 standards into Algebra 1 with a focus on efficiency and mastery. In the spring of 7th grade, buildings host information nights and families meet with math teachers.

**Monitoring Goals (May 2023)**
Growth in students scoring advanced or proficient on MSTEP math, PSAT, and SAT; increased enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade; and stronger problem solving and communication of mathematical thinking measured by internal common assessment.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Presentation Identification**
Middle School Math Update: Board Workshop - January 2026, prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education. The deck reviews the district's middle school mathematics program change, the evidence behind it, perception data collected in May 2025, and current honors enrollment trends.

**TSD Vision for Mathematics**
All students are doers of mathematics. The stated purpose of the mathematics program is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. The vision is attributed to NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

**Findings (May 2023)**
Finding 1, explore curricular changes: program data from the last 5 years preceding COVID revealed that student performance was slightly decreasing or stagnant, and that cohort data showed a decrease in the number of students who achieved at advanced and proficient along with an increase in students who were not proficient. Finding 2, explore course sequencing: students are not able to, or do not, fluidly move between tracks in middle school. Finding 3, explore classroom pedagogy: explore task-based, inquiry-based instruction that builds procedural fluency through conceptual understanding.

**Recommendation: Illustrative Math (May 2023)**
The recommended resource was Illustrative Math, characterized as problem-based; grounded in Universal Design for Learning; with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners; extensions for students who are ready for more; built-in instructional routines that support teachers and students; activity and lesson structure that is predictable and purposeful; and practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review.

**Choosing Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1 (May 2023)**
Math 8 is described as a natural transition from a Math 7 experience, in which students explore ideas of linearity, functions, and geometry and establish a solid foundation for future work in Algebra 1 and Geometry. Honors Algebra 1 embeds Math 8 standards into Algebra 1, with students moving to formalizing and generalizing their understandings with a focus on efficiency and mastery. In the spring of 7th grade, buildings host information nights to discuss and illustrate the differences between Math 8 and Honors Algebra 1 so families can make informed decisions, and families engage with math teachers to discuss individual student needs. Student performance in problem solving skills, communication of mathematical thinking and ideas, math assessment feedback, and standardized test scores should be considered.

**Supporting All Students (May 2023)**
Supports listed include deep levels of learning; investing in staff through professional learning; enrichment materials embedded within Illustrative Math under the Are You Ready For More? feature; enrichment and enhancement opportunities such as Math Club and Robotics; and traditional test-out opportunities to move more quickly through grade levels.

**Monitoring Our Success (May 2023)**
Goal 1: see growth in the number of students who score advanced or proficient on the MSTEP math assessment, PSAT and SAT exams. Goal 2: increase enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade as measured through enrollment data and end of course summative exams. Goal 3: build student problem solving skills and communication of mathematical thinking as monitored through internal common assessment. Measurement of student achievement may include, reported annually, MSTEP/PSAT/SAT including cohort data and math benchmark assessments; and, studied with staff, unit assessments and common assessments, student enrollment in Algebra 1, and student success (grades) in higher levels of mathematics.

**2023 Reflections on Program Change**
The reflections state the intent to align course work with the district vision of deep learning for all students, noting the then-current system does not lend itself to that goal; that the district learned from the field that emphasis should be on depth and fluency, not speed; that the new curriculum provides additional instruction in number sense and procedural fluency and additional access to rich tasks that elicit meaningful discourse and deep understandings; that the new curriculum is designed to offer multiple entry points allowing true differentiation in the general education setting; and that students who desire to accelerate will have the opportunity to reach Algebra 1 by Grade 8 or before, with test-out continuing every spring.

**Student Perception Data (May 2025), n = 1,932**
Celebrations: 93% of students said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% said they had lots of opportunities to interact with each other; 88% agreed that in math class it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% agreed with the statement I know I can be good at math; 79% feel prepared for the next level of math; and 59% said the lessons are just right for them. Challenges: 34% of students would like to receive more specific feedback on how to improve their work; 45% of students do not enjoy learning math; 24% said the lessons are too easy; and 17% said the lessons are too hard.

**Student Voice (May 2025)**
Positive comments quoted include enjoyment of interactions with peers and being at a level where the math is not too easy or too hard; appreciation for a teacher who explains math equations with real life examples; appreciation that there are different ways to learn math; and a student who feels confident enough to raise a hand without being judged and enjoys working with friends, bouncing ideas off them or helping them. Suggestions quoted include adding a difficulty level to assignments to show improvement; more interactive projects or activities so class does not get too boring; a pre-test so the teacher can understand what students know; more repetitive practice per activity to aid retention before tests; and learning more things students will use in real life.

**Teacher Perception Data (May 2025), n = 19**
Celebrations: 95% of teachers say they are comfortable navigating the resource, and 79% say they have the tools they need to accurately measure student progress. Quoted teacher comments praise that there is not just one way to learn or know most of the content, material, skills or strategy and that the curriculum figures out the why; the conceptual content and the different ways of doing math, the Are You Ready For More feature, tasks that are good for students to work together on, and the effort put into getting students to talk and write math; and how the curriculum connects math to real-life situations along with a low floor approach that is inviting for students who may be struggling. Challenges: 37% of teachers need more resources for families and 42% of teachers are using the IM instructional routines that support student access. Quoted concerns include the need for more support for ELD students and students with low reading and comprehension skills, noting that reading a problem three times is not always doable and frequently does not help; requests for more supplemental practice, assessments that match the learning activities, and guidance on what can be combined or eliminated from lessons or units; and a wish for more at-home resources with more written-out examples beyond the online workbook and videos.

**Professional Learning for Middle School Teachers**
2024/25: monthly meetings with Honors Algebra 1, district release professional learning days covering PLCs, UDL, and NWEA learning, building-level PLCs, and support from Math Specialists. 2025/26: district release professional learning days covering PLCs, UDL, and NWEA learning, building-level PLCs, and support from Math Specialists.

**Honors Enrollment Goal and Data**
Under the goal to increase enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade as measured through enrollment data and end of course summative exams, the deck presents 8th Grade Enrollment Trends in Honors Math Courses (Algebra 1 and Above). The chart labels total students as 907, 961, 995, and 1023 across the periods shown. The summary states that the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in student enrollment in honors, and that the district will continue to monitor middle school honors math enrollments. A second chart, Representation of Federal Demographic Categories in Honors Math, carries the values 159, 451, 486, and 348, with population labels n = 1023 and n = 529; the extracted text does not preserve the category labels attached to those values.

**Data To Come**
Future reporting is to include successful completion of Honors Algebra I in 8th grade, measured by course enrollment fall/spring and course enrollment the following year as sequential data; achievement and growth data referencing the November 2025 Board presentation; MSTEP; and NWEA.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: EL Education's Scope of Services Proposal to Troy School District sets out curriculum implementation professional development for an FY27 pilot of the EL Education 6-8 Language Arts curriculum. The package bundles strategic planning, a teacher pilot launch held as half days on August 19th and October 30th, virtual office hours, four in-person coaching days covering the four middle schools piloting the curriculum, and two virtual school-based coaching days. Every element except the teacher pilot launch is offered gratis, with foregone values shown as $6,000, $13,200, and $6,000. The proposal's stated Total Price is $5,000.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Provider and framing**

EL Education, described in the proposal as a leading K-12 education non-profit working to set a higher bar of achievement for America's public schools, offers multi-year partnerships to districts implementing its curriculum. Its portfolio includes a rigorous, intensive K-8 curriculum, classroom-tested teacher resources, professional learning, strategic planning, and coaching focused on leaders and teachers, aimed at meeting the higher bar of national standards, deepening student engagement, and transforming teaching and learning.

**Document title**

DISTRICT IMPLEMENTATION: Curriculum Implementation Professional Development Scope of Services Proposal FY27 Pilot.

**Services and pricing**

| Service | Detail | Price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strategic Planning | 2 days, facilitated in 60-90-minute collaborative planning sessions with the District Leadership Team; in-person meetings plus weekly phone/virtual touchpoints | gratis ($6,000 priced) |
| EL Education 6-8 Language Arts Curriculum: Teacher Pilot Launch | August 19th: 1/2 Day; October 30th: 1/2 Day | $5,000 (in person) |
| Virtual Office Hours w/Teachers + Coaches (Zoom Link) | 4-6 sessions scheduled around middle school schedules; a "Troy School District" landing page of resources | Gratis |
| 4 Coaching Days during Pilot | 1 day at each of the 4 Middle Schools piloting; in person | Gratis ($13,200 priced) |
| Virtual School-Based Coaching Days | 2 days, which can be broken down into 12 hours of support | Gratis ($6,000 priced) |
| **Total Price** | | **$5,000** |

**Delivery details**

Strategic planning sessions are customized, occur with expert EL Education staff members and school/district leadership teams, inform the design of the partnership plan, and occur at critical points in the year to monitor progress on implementation goals and adjust the plan for clarity and alignment with school/district needs.

The teacher pilot launch gives essential learning for those planning to implement the 6-8 ELA curriculum. Through virtual or in-person sessions, participants will describe the structure, design, and key features of the curriculum; identify specific ways it is designed to close the literacy achievement gap; analyze its components to begin planning for instruction; and plan to implement specific instructional practices and strategies that meet the needs of all learners (High Leverage Instructional Practices).

Virtual Office Hours provide structure and consistency, pairing a small professional learning segment with teacher questions. They are to be scheduled when teachers can be paid a stipend to stay after school and no substitute is needed.

During the in-person coaching days, teachers teach a half day and are then released for feedback, action steps, and PD for a half day. EL coaches work with school-based instructional leadership, the implementation team, and teachers on professional learning plans, professional learning development, data analysis, and other implementation supports, guiding partners through strategic planning and goal setting and progress monitoring using the Qualtrics data platform.

The virtual school-based coaching days are delivered to individual schools and designed in alignment with each school's goals and data; the EL Education coach supports building level leaders with data collection and analysis, observes teachers and conducts feedback conversations, and leads grade level planning sessions, with building leaders scheduling the delivery.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Nature of the item**

A Scope of Services Proposal from EL Education presented to the Troy School District Board of Education for its May 19, 2026 meeting. The proposal is headed DISTRICT IMPLEMENTATION: Curriculum Implementation Professional Development Scope of Services Proposal FY27 Pilot, and it prices the professional development wrapper around a pilot of the EL Education 6-8 Language Arts curriculum in the district's middle schools.

**Provider description**

EL Education is characterized as a leading K-12 education non-profit at the forefront of an ambitious movement to set a higher bar of achievement for America's public schools. Through multi-year partnerships, EL Education provides school districts implementing its curriculum with a coordinated set of resources and support intended to ensure sustained implementation and results. Developed from its work with schools, the portfolio of resources includes a rigorous, intensive K-8 curriculum, classroom-tested teacher resources, and practical, inspiring professional learning, strategic planning, and coaching that focus on leaders and teachers. The portfolio of professional services for districts focuses on meeting the higher bar of national standards, deepening student engagement, and transforming teaching and learning to lead to high student achievement.

**Line item 1 - Strategic Planning**

Two days, facilitated in 60-90-minute collaborative planning sessions with the District Leadership Team. The planning sessions are customized and occur with expert EL Education staff members and school/district leadership teams. Sessions inform the design of the partnership plan and occur at critical points in the year to monitor progress on implementation goals and adjust the plan to ensure clarity and alignment with school/district needs. The meetings are a combination of in-person meetings along with weekly phone/virtual touchpoints. Price: gratis ($6,000 priced).

**Line item 2 - EL Education 6-8 Language Arts Curriculum: Teacher Pilot Launch**

Scheduled as August 19th: 1/2 Day and October 30th: 1/2 Day. This comprehensive professional development offering provides essential learning for those planning to implement the 6-8 ELA curriculum. Participants will gain an understanding of the principles behind the curriculum, explain the structure, explore specific ways the curriculum meets all students' needs, and begin planning for instruction. Via engagement in a series of virtual or in-person sessions, participants will be able to: describe the structure, design, and key features of the curriculum; identify specific ways the curriculum is designed to close the literacy achievement gap; analyze the components of the curriculum to begin planning for instruction; and plan to implement specific instructional practices and strategies that meet the needs of all learners (High Leverage Instructional Practices). Price: $5,000 (in person).

**Line item 3 - Virtual Office Hours w/Teachers + Coaches**

Delivered by Zoom link. Virtual Office Hours provide a structure and consistency in which EL Education shares a small professional learning segment and answers questions for teachers. The proposal contemplates setting up 4-6 Virtual Office Hours to occur when best for the dynamic school schedules at the Middle Schools, on days when teachers can be paid a stipend to stay after but do not need a substitute. EL Education will also set up a "Troy School District" landing page for teachers with links to resources, videos, and supports for the curriculum. Price: Gratis.

**Line item 4 - 4 Coaching Days during Pilot**

One day at each of the 4 Middle Schools piloting during the pilot, delivered in person, to support teachers. Teachers will be teaching a half day and then released for feedback, action steps, and PD for a half day. During coaching sessions, EL coaches work with the school-based instructional leadership, implementation team, and teachers to support professional learning plans, professional learning development, data analysis, and additional components of curriculum implementation support. EL coaches guide partners through strategic planning and goal setting and progress monitoring using the Qualtrics data platform, and build the capacity of school-based leadership, teacher leaders, and teachers. Price: Gratis ($13,200 priced).

**Line item 5 - Virtual School-Based Coaching Days**

Two days, which can be broken down into 12 hours of support, delivered virtually, and usable for office hours, planning sessions, or as needed for the schools. These coaching days, delivered to individual schools in the district, will be designed in alignment with the individual school's goals and data. The EL Education coach will support building level leaders with data collection and analysis, observe teachers and conduct feedback conversations, and lead grade level planning sessions. The building leaders will work collaboratively with the EL Education coach to schedule these days for the delivery of ongoing coaching support. Price: Gratis ($6,000 priced).

**Pricing summary**

| Service | Price |
| --- | --- |
| Strategic Planning (2 days) | gratis ($6,000 priced) |
| Teacher Pilot Launch (Aug 19, Oct 30 half days) | $5,000 (in person) |
| Virtual Office Hours w/Teachers + Coaches | Gratis |
| 4 Coaching Days during Pilot | Gratis ($13,200 priced) |
| Virtual School-Based Coaching Days (2 days / 12 hours) | Gratis ($6,000 priced) |
| Total Price | $5,000 |

**Observations**

The only charged component is the in-person teacher pilot launch, and the Total Price line matches that single charge at $5,000. Three of the five services carry a stated priced value that EL Education is waiving, so the proposal documents substantial support offered at no cost alongside the billed launch. The proposal is paginated 1 through 4 and names no signatory, contract term, or purchase order number.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held October 14, 2025 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order at 7:00 p.m. by Vice President Anne with Trustee Philippart absent and adjourned at 8:06 p.m. The Board adopted resolutions recognizing Learning Disabilities Month, Principal Appreciation Month, and fifty-seven 2026 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists, approved a four-item consent agenda, and issued a two-year probationary administrative contract to Saso Vasovski as Technology Director effective October 15, 2025. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Meeting and Attendance
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, October 14, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler were present; Philippart was absent for all recorded votes. Superintendent Machesky attended along with administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Zawislak, Cottone, Vasovski, and Trudel. Approximately 12 members of the audience were present. The meeting adjourned at 8:06 p.m. Minutes were submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (notation EA/jh).

Recognitions
The agenda opened with a TSD Mission Moment and presentation of the Apple Distinguished School Award to Troy Union Elementary and Larson Middle School, a designation held by fewer than a thousand schools worldwide.

Resolutions Adopted
- Learning Disabilities Awareness Month, October 2025: moved by Dr. Melton, supported by Mr. Haupt, noting that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability and joining Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.
- Principal Appreciation Month: moved by Mrs. Zendler, supported by Mrs. Alic, recognizing October as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.
- 2026 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists: moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Zendler, honoring fifty-seven Troy students. More than one million students from some 21,000 high schools entered the program nationally and approximately 16,000 seniors were selected as semifinalists, by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT with comparable SAT scores. A reception was set for November 13th. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

Consent Agenda
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, approving items A through D: minutes of the September 2, 2025 Board Workshop; minutes of the September 16, 2025 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report for August 2025; and second reading and adoption of Board Policy Revisions. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

Personnel
Moved by Mrs. Potts, supported by Mr. Haupt, that the Board issue a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Saso Vasovski, beginning duties as Technology Director on October 15, 2025. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. There were no curriculum items.

Business
- Administration Building furniture purchase, not to exceed $300,000, through pre-existing bid contracts (consortiums), as an expenditure of the 2023 Bond Fund; moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Mrs. Potts. Yes 6, No 0.
- Cafeteria tables for Barnard Elementary awarded to School Specialty in the amount of $46,937.22 from the 2023 Capital Projects Fund; moved by Mrs. Zendler, supported by Mrs. Potts. Yes 6, No 0.
- Technology upgrades and access control bids, moved by Dr. Melton, supported by Mrs. Potts, as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Yes 6, No 0.

Official minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held October 14, 2025 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The minutes carry the notation EA/jh and are signed respectfully submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

CALL TO ORDER AND ATTENDANCE
Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members present were Alic, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Zawislak, Cottone, Vasovski, and Trudel. There were approximately 12 members of the audience. Board member Philippart was recorded absent on every roll call vote of the evening.

RECOGNITION - TSD MISSION MOMENT / APPLE DISTINGUISHED SCHOOLS AWARD
The Board recognized two schools for earning designation as Apple Distinguished Schools, described as a recognition awarded to schools that are centers of innovation, leadership, and educational excellence, demonstrating a clear vision for learning with technology, a culture that supports continuous innovation, and compelling evidence of academic achievement and student engagement. Fewer than a thousand schools worldwide have earned the distinction. The Apple Distinguished School Award was presented to Troy Union Elementary and Larson Middle School, with congratulations to principals, staff, and students.

RECOGNITION - LEARNING DISABILITIES AWARENESS MONTH, OCTOBER 2025
The introduction noted that several national associations dedicated to supporting individuals with learning differences have designated October as a month of awareness, including organizations focused on Dyslexia, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and Down Syndrome; that the U.S. Department of Education has recognized October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / ADHD / Down Syndrome Awareness Month; and that Governor Whitmer declared October as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mr. Haupt to adopt the resolution. The whereas clauses state that the term learning disabilities refers to differences in how brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that learning disabilities range in severity and may impact the acquisition and use of oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and conditions and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that disabilities are a natural part of human diversity though individuals may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths; that specialized assessments and interventions involving home, school, community, and workplace settings can significantly enhance quality of life; that appropriate supports and services allow individuals to achieve their goals and participate fully in society; and that understanding and celebrating unique abilities is essential to an inclusive society embracing the strengths of all Michigan residents. The resolving clause has the Troy School District Board of Education join Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

RECOGNITION - 2025 PRINCIPALS APPRECIATION MONTH
The introduction noted that October has traditionally been celebrated statewide as Principal Appreciation Month in recognition of building-level educational leaders. It was moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses cite that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools, and districts are to ensure all Troy students are college and career ready; that K-12 principals play a vital role in student success and act as liaison between school and community; that Troy School District principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals committed to sound leadership and guidance; and that the district joins educators, parents, and students throughout Michigan to raise awareness of educational leadership. The resolution officially recognizes October as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

RECOGNITION - 2026 NATIONAL MERIT SCHOLARSHIP SEMIFINALISTS
The narrative states that more than one million students nationwide from some 21,000 high schools entered the National Merit Scholarship Program and approximately 16,000 seniors were selected as semifinalists. Troy's fifty-seven semifinalists were named: Hasmita Anil Kumar, Fatima Ateeq, Matthew Batke, Shrish Bhandarkar, Mason Chiew, Sumehra Darafzin, Aarush Das, Arnav Dighrasker, William Dong, Lana Fargaly, Atul Ganesh, Vihaan Gehlaut, Aryan Goswami, Aaroosh Guduguntla, Anusha Gupta, Yeonjoon Ha, Kashifah Hossain, Aafla Ibraheem, Raghav Karur, Ryeo-Won Kim, Shlagha Kompelli, Aarush Kulkarni, Iniya Kumar, Ria Lattupalli, Phuong Le, Seungheon Lee, Sophia Li, Abigail Losey, Jing-Yi Ma, Jeeva Maridass, Joel Matthew, Aasrith Modem, Michael Molenda, Pratyush Neelakantan, Sameer Pai, Aayushi Parab, Kanghee Park, Sanjana Prabhu, Kristin Prakash, Akshiithi Prithiviraj, Tejaaswin Raja, Hansini Ramini, Sahas Ravoor, Ashwin Shrivastav, Divya Sovani, Chinmay Sujith Nair, Saanvi Thippireddy, Julia Triculescu, Yunis Turk, Matthew Vijayasegar, Akein Weerakoon, Anthony Wu, Casey Xin, Jonathan Xu, Alice Yang, Angela Zhang, and Eric Zhou. Copies of the resolution were to be presented to the students at a reception on November 13th. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Zendler. The resolution notes that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test (PSAT) and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS; PUBLIC COMMUNICATION ON AGENDA ITEMS
Both were recorded as None.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA
It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the September 2, 2025 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the September 16, 2025 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - August 2025; and Second Reading and Adoption - Board Policy Revisions. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

It was moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board of Education issue a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Saso Vasovski, who will begin his duties as Technology Director on October 15, 2025. Purpose and Framing
Presented to the TSD Board of Education in November 2025 under the title "Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action." Stated purposes: student performance on state assessments and how performance has changed over time; district-by-district performance; performance gaps between student groups; and areas of focus and celebrations. The deck notes that state assessments are summative snapshots, one part of a balanced assessment system, useful to policy and decision makers for identifying schools, groups, and students for support, and are not designed to be diagnostic or drive day-to-day teaching and learning.

M-STEP Grades 3-7, Percent Advanced or Proficient

| Grade | ELA 2025 | ELA 2024 | Math 2025 | Math 2024 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| 7 | 66.1 | 64.8 | 68.4 | 66.0 |

Grades 3-7 Proficiency Over Time

| Series | SY 19 | SY 22 | SY 23 | SY 24 | SY 25 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ELA TSD | 74.0% | 69.1% | 65.9% | 63.2% | 67.9% |
| ELA Oakland | 53.3% | 51.4% | 52.0% | 50.2% | 49.8% |
| ELA Statewide | 45.1% | 41.6% | 40.9% | 39.6% | 38.9% |
| Math TSD | 75.0% | 74.6% | 73.1% | 72.4% | 77.9% |
| Math Oakland | 57.3% | 53.6% | 54.8% | 55.9% | 55.4% |
| Math Statewide | 46.7% | 41.5% | 42.9% | 43.4% | 42.7% |

County comparison bars for grades 3-7 show 71%, 70%, 67%, 66%, 66%, and 62% in ELA and 71%, 70%, 68%, 68%, and 65% in math.

PSAT 8 and SAT 11
ELA: 84.2% grade 8 and 77.3% grade 11 in 2024; 83.5% and 79.3% in 2025. Math: 64.3% grade 8 and 59.5% grade 11 in 2024; 64.3% and 60.7% in 2025. Eighth grade ELA over time for TSD: 87.1%, 81.0%, 85.6%, 84.2%, 83.5% across SY 19 through SY 25, versus Oakland 72.5%, 69.5%, 71.4%, 74.4%, 74.5% and statewide 61.9%, 59.7%, 59.7%, 64.5%, 65.3%. Eighth grade math TSD: 75.1%, 67.5%, 69.1%, 64.3%, 64.3%; Oakland 55.1%, 47.6%, 49.0%, 45.9%, 42.4%; statewide 41.4%, 36.2%, 36.3%, 32.6%, 30.4%. Eleventh grade ELA TSD: 82.9%, 75.3%, 76.9%, 77.3%, 79.3%; math TSD: 73.6%, 61.6%, 61.3%, 59.5%, 60.7%.

M-STEP Science and Social Studies (Grades 5, 8, 11)
Science 2025: 61.1%, 65.3%, 50.2%; 2024: 62.6%, 64.4%, 46.3%. Social studies 2025: 51.0%, 68.1%, 56.9%; 2024: 34.9%, 47.5%, 46.6%.

Gap Analysis
The deck frames the performance gap, also called an opportunity gap, for students with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners. Multi-Tiered System of Support actions include coherence building, Professional Learning Communities at all schools, universal supports, progress monitoring for students on a plan, a district handbook, interventions taught by content-strong teachers, and a focus on Tier 1 instruction. Special education is called the largest and most persistent achievement gap; economically disadvantaged students outperform state and county peers though fewer than half meet proficiency; English learners perform strongly against county and state peers with a gap remaining.

Celebrations
Third grade ranked first in the county in both ELA and math, with a spring 2025 third grade ELA proficiency chart topped at 67.9%. Troy Public Schools ranked fourth statewide with 108 Seals of Biliteracy in 2024-25. AP students scoring 3 or higher rose across five years to 89.0% in 2024-25, and AP English 11 enrollment reached 45.3% of eleventh graders in 2025-2026. Middle school honors math enrollment was reported at 22% of grades 6-8 in both 24/25 and 25/26.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education dated November 2025, titled "Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action." The stated purposes for the evening were student performance on state assessments and how performance has changed over time, district-by-district performance, performance gaps between student groups, and areas of focus and celebrations.

ABOUT THESE DATA
The deck explains that state assessments are summative assessments designed to be a snapshot in time of student performance; that they are one part of a balanced assessment system that uses multiple and varied assessments to provide all users with information they need to support teaching and learning; that they help policy makers and decision makers understand overall levels of achievement and identify schools, groups, and students for support; and that they are not designed to be diagnostic or drive day-to-day teaching and learning.

M-STEP GRADES 3-7, PERCENT ADVANCED OR PROFICIENT
ELA by grade (3, 4, 5, 6, 7), 2025: 67.9, 66.3, 67.9, 64.5, 66.1. ELA 2024: 63.2, 66.8, 69.0, 64.4, 64.8. Math 2025: 77.9, 65.9, 65.5, 65.8, 68.4. Math 2024: 72.4, 68.9, 64.1, 66.3, 66.0.

M-STEP 3-7 PROFICIENCY OVER TIME (SY 19, SY 22, SY 23, SY 24, SY 25)
ELA: TSD 74.0%, 69.1%, 65.9%, 63.2%, 67.9%; Oakland 53.3%, 51.4%, 52.0%, 50.2%, 49.8%; Statewide 45.1%, 41.6%, 40.9%, 39.6%, 38.9%. Math: TSD 75.0%, 74.6%, 73.1%, 72.4%, 77.9%; Oakland 57.3%, 53.6%, 54.8%, 55.9%, 55.4%; Statewide 46.7%, 41.5%, 42.9%, 43.4%, 42.7%. In both subjects the Troy line sits well above the Oakland County and statewide lines across every year shown.

M-STEP 3-7 COUNTY COMPARISON
The ELA grades 3-7 percent at or above proficiency bar chart displays district values of 71%, 70%, 67%, 66%, 66%, and 62%. The math grades 3-7 chart displays 71%, 70%, 68%, 68%, and 65%.

PSAT 8 / SAT 11 ELA AND MATH
ELA: grade 8 84.2% and grade 11 77.3% in 2024; grade 8 83.5% and grade 11 79.3% in 2025. Math: grade 8 64.3% and grade 11 59.5% in 2024; grade 8 64.3% and grade 11 60.7% in 2025.

EIGHTH GRADE PROFICIENCY OVER TIME (SY 19, SY 22, SY 23, SY 24, SY 25)
ELA: TSD 87.1%, 81.0%, 85.6%, 84.2%, 83.5%; Oakland 72.5%, 69.5%, 71.4%, 74.4%, 74.5%; Statewide 61.9%, 59.7%, 59.7%, 64.5%, 65.3%. Math: TSD 75.1%, 67.5%, 69.1%, 64.3%, 64.3%; Oakland 55.1%, 47.6%, 49.0%, 45.9%, 42.4%; Statewide 41.4%, 36.2%, 36.3%, 32.6%, 30.4%.

PSAT 8 COUNTY COMPARISON
ELA PSAT 8 percent at or above proficiency bars: 89%, 89%, 89%, 88%, 85%, 83%, 65%. Math PSAT 8 percent at or above proficiency bars: 70%, 64%, 64%, 63%, 60%, 30%.

ELEVENTH GRADE PROFICIENCY OVER TIME (SY 19, SY 22, SY 23, SY 24, SY 25)
ELA: TSD 82.9%, 75.3%, 76.9%, 77.3%, 79.3%; Oakland 63.1%, 59.5%, 59.5%, 60.0%, 64.1%; Statewide 55.3%, 51.6%, 52.2%, 51.3%, 55.4%. Math: TSD 73.6%, 61.6%, 61.3%, 59.5%, 60.7%; Oakland 46.5%, 39.4%, 39.1%, 35.6%, 37.4%; Statewide 36.3%, 30.0%, 29.9%, 26.3%, 27.5%.

SAT COUNTY COMPARISON
SAT Evidence Based Reading and Writing, grade 11 percent proficient: 85.1, 82.5, 82.3, 81.8, 79.3, 75.6, 55.4. SAT Math, grade 11 percent proficient: 64.7, 60.7, 58.9, 56.6, 56.5, 27.5.

M-STEP SCIENCE, GRADES 5, 8, AND 11
2025 percent advanced or proficient: 61.1%, 65.3%, 50.2%. 2024 percent advanced or proficient: 62.6%, 64.4%, 46.3%.

M-STEP SOCIAL STUDIES, GRADES 5, 8, AND 11
2025 percent advanced or proficient: 51.0%, 68.1%, 56.9%. 2024 percent advanced or proficient: 34.9%, 47.5%, 46.6%. All three grades show marked increases from the prior year.

GAP ANALYSIS - IMPLICATIONS AND ACTIONS
The deck states that historically districts have struggled to raise the performance of students with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners on par with countywide and statewide rates of performance, commonly known as the performance gap, and that some refer to this as an opportunity gap wherein certain student groups have not been afforded adequate opportunities and support to perform on par with statewide and countywide peers.

MULTI-TIERED SYSTEM OF SUPPORT
Listed elements: district commitment to building coherence, in process; focus on systems that support all students; commitment to Professional Learning Communities, in process at all schools; universal supports; review of progress monitoring for any student on a plan; development of a district handbook; interventions taught by content strong teachers; and focus on Tier 1 instruction.

PERFORMANCE GAPS 2025 - SPECIAL EDUCATION
Values shown by Grade 3, Grade 5, Grade 6, Grade 7, Grade 8, and Grade 11. ELA special education: 45.4, 49.4, 47.7, 49.8, 52.3, 53.1. Math special education: 39.1, 40.9, 46.7, 49.3, 54.1, 51.7.

PERFORMANCE GAPS 2025 - ECONOMICALLY DISADVANTAGED
Values shown by Grade 3, Grade 5, Grade 6, Grade 7, Grade 8, and Grade 11. ELA economically disadvantaged: 29.5, 24.2, 30.8, 27.2, 20.8, 25.7. Math economically disadvantaged: 22.6, 28.4, 32, 35.2, 41.4, 40.1.

ANALYSIS - STRENGTHS TO BUILD ON
TSD consistently outperforms county and state averages, demonstrating strong and effective instructional practices; all subgroups (economically disadvantaged, special education, English learners) are performing above their statewide peers, indicating effective support systems; performance stability over three years underscores the resilience and sustainability of current practices; and third grade ranked first in the county in ELA and math.

ANALYSIS - FOCUS AREAS FOR CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT
Special education represents the largest and most persistent achievement gap, with continued focus on inclusive practices and Tier 1 instruction and targeted interventions provided by content strong teachers. Economically disadvantaged students, while outperforming state and county peers, have fewer than half meeting proficiency and remain a critical area for support and targeted strategies and interventions. English learners show strong performance in comparison to county and state peers, yet a performance gap remains, and ongoing support for language acquisition and academic language development is described as essential.

MIDDLE SCHOOL MATH PERFORMANCE UPDATES
A cohort slide for the current 9th grade, Class of 2029, notes it is the last split cohort with a 6/7 and 7/8 track and IM 6/7, and the first cohort with choice after 7th grade of Honors Algebra 1; cohort performance figures shown are 65%, 63%, 68%, 68% and 62%, 65%, 66%, 65%, with accompanying counts 15, 13, 16, 11 and 23, 21, 18, 24. Percent of middle school students enrolled in Honors Algebra 1: 13.1%, 12.7%, 12.0%, 19.8%, 17.3%. Honors Geometry: 2.08%, 1.66%, 1.87%, 1.30%, 2.93%. Honors Algebra 2: 0.81%, 0.76%, 0.20%, 1.10%, 1.90%. Grades 6-8 combined: 21/22 16%, 22/23 15%, 23/24 14%, 24/25 22%, 25/26 22%. The slide states that middle school enrollment in high school honors math has increased by 6% over the last 5 years, representing an additional 175 middle school students annually in 24/25 and 25/26 who have enrolled in honors level math.

CELEBRATIONS - THIRD GRADE ELA AND MATH
A spring 2025 third grade ELA proficiency ranking chart lists district values of 67.9%, 66.6%, 65.6%, 63.1%, 61.6%, 61.5%, 58.6%, 54.1%, 51.3%, 50.5%, 48.7%, 48.4%, 48.1%, 47.3%, 45.9%, 44.9%, 42.7%, 41.6%, 40.6%, 39.6%, 38.9%, 37.0%, 34.8%, 33.8%, and 21.0%. Slides declare TSD third grade first in county in ELA and first in county in math.

CELEBRATIONS - 2024-25 SEAL OF BILITERACY
Counts by district: Detroit Public School Community District 162; Grand Rapids Public Schools 126; Portage Public Schools 112; Troy Public Schools 108; Forest Hills Public Schools 106; Lincoln Park, School District of the City of 99; Dearborn City School District 90; Utica Community Schools 70; West Ottawa Public Schools District 70; Hamtramck, School District of the City of 69. The deck explains the Seal of Biliteracy recognizes students who have achieved proficiency in English and at least one additional language and highlights strong communication skills, cultural awareness, and academic achievement. Reasons it matters: gives students a competitive edge for college admissions and scholarships; supports career readiness by validating bilingual skills valued in the global workforce; honors and celebrates the linguistic and cultural diversity of students; and encourages continued language learning and cultural competence.

CELEBRATIONS - AP ENROLLMENT AND PERFORMANCE
AP students scoring 3 or higher: 82.5% in 2020-21, 84.6% in 2021-22, 87.3% in 2022-23, 86.6% in 2023-24, and 89.0% in 2024-25. OTHER SECTIONS

Meeting and Attendance
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, November 18, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Also present were Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Potts and Zendler; Superintendent Machesky; and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Recker, Milanov, Pawlus, Crowe and Trudel. Approximately 30 members of the audience attended. The meeting adjourned at 9:08 p.m. Minutes submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary. Reference line EA/jh.

Recognitions
Wass Elementary School was honored for its designation as a National Blue-Ribbon School. Because the U.S. Department of Education discontinued the national program, the State of Michigan took over recognizing 2025 Blue Ribbon Schools; Wass was one of 13 public schools in Michigan named. Interim State Superintendent Dr. Sue C. Carnell and State Board President Dr. Pamela Pugh were quoted. Wass was recognized at a Lansing ceremony on November 13; Principal Kristin Crowe and staff came forward. The Communications Department was recognized for 17 National School and Public Relations Association (NSPRA) awards and 5 Michigan School and Public Relations Association (MSPRA) awards. Melissa Verduyn, Thomas Butcher, Adam Burns and Alison Hendry were thanked.

Consent Agenda
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, to approve items A through D: minutes of the October 7, 2025 Board Workshop; minutes of the October 14, 2025 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report for September 2025; and a garage door purchase for Troy High School. Yes 7, No 0. Additions and deletions, agenda-item public communication, personnel items, and other business were all recorded as None.

Curriculum
Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Instruction Kris Griffor and Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction Christine DiPilato reported on state assessment performance over time, district-by-district comparisons and gaps between student groups, covering M-STEP, PSAT and SAT results in math, ELA, science and social studies, plus Seal of Biliteracy and AP enrollment and performance. Dr. Recker, Director of Teaching and Learning, previewed the District's new Data Dashboard.

| 2024/2025 audit | Accept audited 2025 financial statements from Plante Moran; moved Anne, supported Alic | 7-0 |
| Series II bonds | Authorize 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds not to exceed $220,000,000; moved Zendler, supported Haupt | 7-0 |
| iPads | Purchase iPads and cases from Apple, $433,950.00, Capital Projects Fund; moved Haupt, supported Anne | 7-0 |
| Technology systems | Bid to TEL Systems, Inc., $384,610.17, 2023 Capital Projects Fund; moved Alic, supported Potts | 7-0 |
| Traffic signal, Smith MS | Bid to J. Ranck Electric, $494,694.00, 2023 Capital Projects Fund; moved Potts, supported Anne | 7-0 |
| ELD materials | Language Power ELD curriculum, $104,509.12, General Fund, with $82,681.38 funded through Title III; moved Alic, supported Potts | 7-0 |

Bond Detail
The $555,000,000 bond issue was passed by voters on November 8, 2022. The District proposed issuing the second series under that proposal in an amount not to exceed $193,000,000 and refunding the 2016 School Building and Site Bonds in an amount not to exceed $27,000,000, combined into a single series not to exceed $220,000,000 to reduce issuance and administration cost. Dr. Richard Machesky and Dan Trudel were authorized to accept a purchase offer.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Presentation to the Troy Board of Education workshop of December 9, 2025 recommending adoption of new AP Spanish and AP French resources from Vista Higher Learning. The current materials, Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, were adopted in 2017, lack current cultural content and AP test preparation, and in the French case are a Level 4 textbook rather than an AP text. Vista was selected over Wayside and Klett because its rigor matches the AP exam, its authors are College Board trainers, and it holds 80 percent of the AP World Languages market share.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Purpose
AP Spanish and AP French resource adoption, presented at the 12/9/25 Board Workshop of the Troy School District.

Context and Rationale
The World Language sequence runs Level 1 through Level 5 AP, and the AP exams are written at the intermediate high and advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision describes learners who can communicate in an ever-expanding global community, discover and experience the heritage of another culture, become resilient risk-takers able to adapt to new environments, improve memory and problem-solving skills, enhance college applications and professional marketability, and open themselves to world travel. AP World Language and Culture is described as equivalent to an intermediate-level college course, in which students apply interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication while exploring family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The exam assesses both language and culture, but the resources adopted in 2017 do not represent current culture.

Current State
World Languages operates on a 7-year adoption cycle. Under the PLC structure, Troy AP World Language teachers want a common resource to build cohesion among programs. Current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, with outdated readings that are not updated, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, which is a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources. Teachers currently pull materials from a wide variety of sources, some at their own cost.

Selection Process
Guided by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. Timeline: exploration of resources during the 24-25 school year; 8/11 leadership planning; 8/20 department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7 rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20 pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18 PLC planning and check-ins; 12/2 pilot feedback and synthesis.

Vendors Considered
| Vendor | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Wayside | French and Spanish; relatable content with a variety of authentic resources, but does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and is only a textbook without assessment practice |
| Klett | No AP resource for French; Spanish has many authentic resources and AP practice but does not represent AP rigor, has fewer resources than Vista, and less user-friendly technology |
| Vista Higher Learning | French and Spanish; matches the rigor of the AP exam, culturally relevant resources and a large resource bank; resources may need scaffolding at the start of the year |

Recommended Resource
Vista Higher Learning. Its authors are also College Board trainers, and Vista holds 80 percent of the AP World Languages market share. The 26-27 AP exam will be updated; Vista agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year and, when it updates its textbooks, to provide updated electronic and physical resources free of cost. The district will bank its professional learning credit to support the change in August. Sample features shown included AP French culturally relevant resources with student supports, an AP Spanish cultural comparison in which a student named Maya contrasts the role of grandparents in the United States and El Salvador, and AP Spanish simulated conversations, a free response task; interpersonal communication practice supports the Free Response AP tasks, which are 50 percent of the exam.

Stakeholder Support and Timeline
Student quotations praised the online textbook for offering more listening and speaking resources, easier navigation, iPad access and speaking practice that built confidence for the heavily weighted speaking sections of the AP test. Student and caretaker surveys were referenced, followed by a financial request slide. Anticipated timeline: December, order placed; January, physical materials inventoried and pilot licenses extended into June; August, 7-year licenses begin and are rostered, with PD from Vista covering College Board changes.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board workshop presentation titled AP Spanish and AP French Resource Adoption, delivered at the 12/9/25 Troy School District Board Workshop, proposing replacement of the district's AP world language instructional materials.

CONTEXT AND RATIONALE. The presentation situates AP within the district's world language sequence of Level 1, Level 2, Level 3, Level 4 and Level 5 AP, noting that the AP exams are written at the intermediate high and advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision states that world language learners can communicate in an ever-expanding global community; discover and experience the rich heritage of another culture; become resilient risk-takers with a greater capacity to adapt to new environments; improve their memory and problem-solving skills for better overall academic performance; enhance their college applications and increase their professional marketability; and open themselves to opportunities for world travel. The AP World Languages vision is quoted as describing AP World Language and Culture as equivalent to an intermediate-level college course in which students cultivate their understanding of language and culture by applying interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication in real-life situations while exploring concepts related to family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The presentation stresses that the exam assesses both language and culture, but that the resources adopted in 2017 do not have current culture represented.

CURRENT STATE. World Languages follows a 7-year adoption cycle. With the PLC structure in place, Troy AP World Language teachers desire a common resource to help build cohesion among programs. The current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, criticized for outdated readings that have not been updated, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, which is identified as a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources that have not been updated. The stated current reality is that teachers are doing their best to pull resources from a wide variety of sources, some even at their own cost.

PROCESS OF RESOURCE SELECTION. Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant, supported the process. The AP resources timeline was: 24-25 school year, exploration of resources; 8/11, leadership planning; 8/20, department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7, rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20, pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18, PLC planning and check-ins; and 12/2, pilot feedback and synthesis.

AP VENDORS CONSIDERED, PROS AND CONS. Wayside was evaluated for both French and Spanish; while the resource has relatable content for students with a variety of authentic resources, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and is only a textbook without assessment practice. Klett has no AP resource for French; for Spanish, while the resource has many authentic resources and AP practice, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment, does not have the number of resources that Vista has, and its technology was less user friendly. Vista Higher Learning was evaluated for both French and Spanish and was found to match the rigor of the AP exam, providing meaningful, culturally relevant resources as well as a large resource bank; because of that rigor, resources may need to be scaffolded at the start of the year. Additional points favoring Vista: the authors of Vista are also College Board trainers; Vista has 80 percent of the AP World Languages market share; the 26-27 AP exam will be updated and Vista has agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year; when Vista updates its textbooks it will provide the district updated electronic and physical resources free of cost; and the district will bank its professional learning credit to support this change in August.

FEATURES OF THE RECOMMENDED TEXTS. Illustrative slides covered AP French culturally relevant resources, and AP French culturally relevant resources with student supports. For AP Spanish, a cultural comparison example was shown: on the AP test students must compare the country they are studying with the United States, and in the sample a student named Maya shares how the role of grandparents differs in the United States versus El Salvador. Another example showed AP Spanish simulated conversations, described as a free response task on the AP exam. The presentation notes that this is an example of interpersonal communication that fosters student confidence and practice for the Free Response AP tasks, which constitute 50 percent of the exam.

ADDITIONAL STAKEHOLDER SUPPORT. Two student quotations were included. One student said they like an online textbook because it has more resources such as listening and speaking, they can navigate the pages better and faster, and it is easier to have the textbook on an iPad. A second student said they have used the ebook many times in class and the variety of resources has been really helpful; that the hardest part of learning Spanish at this level is being able to speak their thoughts; that the ebook gave them speaking practice that already allowed them to feel more confident about their speaking abilities; and that the speaking sections of the AP test are huge, very important to the overall score and heavily weighted, so having these resources builds confidence in trying to get a good score. Slides for a Student Survey and a Caretaker Survey followed.

FINANCIAL REQUEST AND TIMELINE. A financial request section was included in the deck. The anticipated timeline moving forward is: December, order placed; January, physical materials inventoried and pilot licenses extended into June; August, 7-year licenses begin and are rostered, with professional development from Vista covering the College Board changes. The presentation closes with a questions slide.

MEMORANDUM AND RECOMMENDATION. The memorandum states that the factors considered were current enrollment across the Troy School District; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of Schools of Choice siblings who would be age-eligible to enter the district in 2026-2027 if the decision is made to admit a limited number of kindergarten, first and sixth through eighth grade students under Schools of Choice; and available elementary classrooms. After analyzing the data, administration recommends that the district use Plante Moran Realpoint enrollment projection numbers as the foundation for determining the number of Schools of Choice students to admit for the 2026-2027 school year, and accept Schools of Choice applications for kindergarten at 83 under Section 105 and 4 under Section 105C; first grade at 25 under Section 105 and 1 under Section 105C; and sixth to eighth grade combined at 2 under Section 105 and 1 under Section 105c. Based upon the number of applications to kindergarten received for the 2025-2026 school year, administration anticipates attracting many more than 12 sibling preference survey response applicants, which would allow the district to admit 87 kindergarteners. Middle school students would be placed in a building according to available space.
