**What it is**
A Troy School District administration update to the Board of Education for the April 28, 2026 workshop, titled "MS Math Update Survey Feedback March 2026." It reviews the middle school math curriculum and progression change adopted in May 2023, presents March 2026 survey and listening-session feedback, and closes with five recommended next steps.

**Historical context and commitments**
Big Ideas was described as outdated and not aligned to the district's vision for math. At adoption the administration committed to annual review of achievement data (MSTEP/PSAT), annual review of Honors Alg 1 enrollment data, annual feedback collection, implementation of NWEA, ongoing teacher support, and continued MTSS building. The Board committed to reviewing annual data sets and understanding a 3-5 year implementation timeline, noting that adoption "does not require a 7 year cycle if other concerns arise." The adoption cycle has four stages: Research & Vision, Explore, Implementation, and Curriculum Review Cycle.

**Achievement and enrollment data**
MSTEP results have been reviewed annually for grades 6 and 7: 6th grade 2024 (first year of implementation data), 6th grade 2025 (second year), and 7th grade 2025 (first year). No 8th grade PSAT 2026 achievement data is available yet for the first fully implemented cohort. The MSTEP slide carries n-values of 567, 607, 643, 576, 642 and 677. A slide on 8th grade honors math enrollment (Algebra 1 and above) lists totals of 907, 961, 995 and 1023 students and concludes the sequence change increased honors enrollment.

**Survey participation**

| Survey group | Participation count | Percent of population |
|---|---|---|
| Student Survey | 2,059 | 72% |
| Parent/Guardian Survey | 398 | 14% |
| Staff Survey | 21 | 81% |

A later slide reports a final parent participation total of 408 respondents, of whom 214 (52.5%) gave open-ended feedback on the curriculum and 152 (37.3%) on the progression model.

**Staff themes (n=21)**
Progression model: too much content in Honors Algebra 1 combined with Math 8, 7 (33.3%); difficulty with differentiation, 5 (23.8%); underchallenged students, 5 (23.8%); fear of lower outcomes for Algebra 1 students, 4 (19.0%). Illustrative Mathematics curriculum: insufficient materials/practice problems, 12 (57.1%); not enough scaffolding or differentiation, 8 (38.1%); pacing too fast, 7 (33.3%); Algebra 1 content combined with Math 8, 7 (33.3%); too much focus on story problems, 4 (19.0%); negative CoTeach AI experience, 4 (19.0%). On the progression overall: revisit/revise, 11 (52.4%); no opinion stated, 8 (38.1%); favorable, 1 (4.8%); mixed, 1 (4.8%).

**Parent and student themes**
Parent themes: more practice problems, homework or parent-friendly at-home resources (93 responses); physical textbooks and less technology/AI/screen time (87 responses); more rigor, earlier honors options and acceleration (75 responses). Students (2,059 responses) most enjoyed peer collaboration (491), the challenge of new concepts (480) and supportive teachers (390); recommended changes were no change or unsure (301), pacing changes (247) and clearer materials (209).

**Listening sessions and celebrations**
Sessions were held at each of the four middle schools with 27 of 28 teachers participating, covering curriculum, progression and timeline. Throughlines: affirm Illustrative Mathematics as Tier 1 but add resources; vertical alignment grades 5-8; the Honors Alg 1 structure including Math 8 is challenging; at-home practice and parent supports are needed. Celebrations cited a higher percentage of students in honors/accelerated math in 8th and 9th grade than before 2024, consistent MSTEP improvement over three years, and 93% of middle school students reporting they feel they can be good at math.

**Recommended next steps**
(1) Honors Alg 1 work group beginning summer 2026, continuing through 26/27; (2) create or purchase at-home learning resources, summer 2026; (3) vertical alignment work group on 5th and 6th grade learning targets, summer 2026; (4) pilot Accelerated Math 6/7 for fall 2026, with parent nights the week of 5/4, an opt-in structure and a maintained test-out option for Math 6; (5) ongoing 26/27 work on "on ramps" and "off ramps," with a recommendation to the Board in early spring (March/April 2027).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Troy School District administration presentation to the Board of Education for the April 28, 2026 workshop, titled "MS Math Update Survey Feedback March 2026." It reports on the middle school mathematics curriculum and course progression the Board adopted in May 2023, summarizes survey and listening-session feedback gathered in March 2026, and sets out five recommended next steps.

HISTORICAL CONTEXT. The change was driven by outdated math materials and a former curriculum, Big Ideas, that "did not align to vision for math." Board adoption of the new curriculum and new progression occurred in May 2023. TSD Administration committed to annual review of student achievement data (MSTEP/PSAT); annual review of student course enrollment data (Honors Alg 1); annual collection of feedback from staff, students and families; implementation of NWEA; investment in ongoing teacher support; and continuing to build MTSS structures. The Board committed to reviewing annual data sets and understanding the implementation timeline, described as 3-5 years, with the note that "adoption does not require a 7 year cycle if other concerns arise."

CURRICULUM ADOPTION AND IMPLEMENTATION CYCLE. Four stages are described: Research & Vision (research best instructional practices, review state standards, align with the TSD strategic plan, examine district data trends); Explore (propose resources for early-adopter and pilot teams, assemble a curriculum review team, gather data on engagement, performance, joy and usability); Implementation (implement as recommended by the curriculum review and math leadership teams and seek School Board approval, supported by professional learning, job-embedded coaching and classroom visits); and Curriculum Review Cycle (continue professional learning through in-district, local and national partnerships and adjust based on data).

ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT DATA. MSTEP data has been reviewed annually for 6th and 7th grade: MSTEP 6th grade 2024 (first year of implementation data), MSTEP 6th grade 2025 (second year of 6th grade implementation data), and MSTEP 7th grade 2025 (first year of implementation data). For PSAT 8th grade 2026, no academic achievement data is available yet for 8th grade, described as the first cohort to have full implementation of the new program. The achievement slide lists n-values of 567, 607, 643, 576, 642 and 677.

HONORS ENROLLMENT. A slide titled "8th Grade Enrollment Trends in Honors Math Courses (Algebra 1 and Above)" reports total students of 907, 961, 995 and 1023, and states the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in honors enrollment, which the district will continue to monitor.

SURVEY PURPOSE AND PARTICIPATION. The district surveyed middle school students, parents/guardians and math teachers on instructional practices in math classrooms, curriculum implementation of Illustrative Mathematics, student learning, and middle school math course progression. Participation was: Student Survey 2,059 respondents, 72% of the population; Parent/Guardian Survey 398, 14%; Staff Survey 21, 81%.

STAFF SURVEY RESPONSES (n=21). On student experience, 7 respondents (33.3%) said most students understand the goals of lessons because the work is at the right level for them; 7 (33.3%) said most students feel lost even after asking questions or reviewing material; 1 (4.8%) said most students are underchallenged and would like more opportunities for advanced work. Combination responses each drew 2 respondents (9.5%): understand-plus-underchallenged; underchallenged-plus-feel-lost; and all three statements together. The parallel student and parent items read "I usually understand the goals of the lesson because the work is at the right level for me," "I feel underchallenged by lessons," and "I feel lost even after asking questions or reviewing material."

STAFF-IDENTIFIED AREAS OF IMPROVEMENT. Main themes within the current math progression model: Too Much Content in Honors Algebra 1 (Combined with Math 8), 7 (33.3%); Difficulty with Differentiation (Pacing, Learning Gaps, and Student Supports), 5 (23.8%); Underchallenged Students, 5 (23.8%); Fear of Lower Outcomes for Algebra 1 Students, 4 (19.0%). Main themes within the current Illustrative Mathematics (IM) curriculum: Insufficient Materials (Practice Problems), 12 (57.1%); Not Enough Scaffolding/Differentiation Within Curriculum, 8 (38.1%); Curriculum Pacing (Too Fast), 7 (33.3%); Concerns about Algebra 1 Content combined with Math 8 (Lower Rigor and Too Much Content), 7 (33.3%); Too Much Focus on Story Problems, 4 (19.0%); Negative CoTeach AI Experience, 4 (19.0%). Math teacher perspective on the progression: Revisit/Revise the Math Progression Model, 11 (52.4%); No Opinion Stated, 8 (38.1%); Favorable View, 1 (4.8%); Mixed View, 1 (4.8%).

AI SUMMARY. A CoPilot-generated executive summary of the teacher survey reports significant concerns about both the IM curriculum and the course progression model, particularly pacing, differentiation, foundational skill gaps, and Algebra 1 in 8th grade, with a prevailing tone that is negative to mixed. Its takeaways: IM philosophy has merit but materials are insufficient on their own; foundational skills and fluency require far more emphasis; differentiation is difficult without structural changes; Algebra 1 in 8th grade is a critical pain point; teachers want clear learning targets, flexible pacing and defined pathways rather than scripted constraints.

STATUS AS OF 4/7/26. Next steps recorded from the prior update: additional time to review feedback, collaborate with the team and prepare a recommendation to the Board at the 4/28 workshop. Anticipated topics were adoption of supplemental resources, convening a curriculum review team inclusive of MS math teachers, and exploring accelerated pathways, with board consideration of a formal recommendation in winter/spring 2027 for implementation in fall of 2027.

PARENT SURVEY UPDATE. Final survey participation total: 408 parent respondents. Of the 408, 214 provided an open response about the current math curriculum and 152 about the current course progression model; the remainder left the open response blank. As a share of the 408 total responses, curriculum feedback was 52.5% and progression feedback 37.3%. Parent Theme #1, a desire for more practice problems, homework or parent-friendly resources for home use, drew 93 responses. Parent Theme #2, a desire for physical textbooks, more paper-pencil work, and less technology/AI or screen time, drew 87 responses. Parent Theme #3, a desire for more rigor, earlier honors track options and additional acceleration, drew 75 responses, including "There should be honors or advanced options instead of forcing students to skip an entire grade."

STUDENT RESPONSES. From 2,059 total responses to "What I enjoy about math class": Peer Collaboration and Social Interaction, 491 responses; Enjoying the Challenge and Learning New Concepts, 480; Supportive and Engaging Teachers, 390. From 2,059 total responses on recommended changes: No Changes Needed or Not Sure, 301; Pacing Changes Within the Curriculum, 247; and Clearer Materials, Explanations, and Instructions, 209, including a comment that "the homework, textbook, and teacher slides don't match up."

TEACHER LISTENING SESSIONS. Held at each of the 4 middle schools with 27/28 teachers participating, covering curriculum (Illustrative Math), math course progression (Math 6, Math 7, Math 8/Hon Alg 1), and recommended timeline. Middle School A teachers wanted to continue with IM but with publisher-aligned practice problems and assessments, saw room for more rigor in 6th grade, and said students are skimming Pre-Algebra content in Honors Algebra 1; a majority said the progression is not working at the Math 8/Hon Alg 1 level, though they were concerned about sorting students in 6th grade, and asked whether a condensed IM Math 6/7 could serve as Tier 1 for all incoming 6th graders. Middle School B teachers said IM builds conceptual knowledge but has insufficient materials ("Maintain IM with more support"), that parents struggle because workbooks do not go home, that pacing is "intense," and that combining Math 8 and Algebra 1 in one course is a major challenge; a majority said the progression needs to change, with interest in Math 6/7 and Math 7/8. At Middle School C, some 8th grade and honors Algebra 1 teachers felt IM was "not the right selection" and that students were missing content previously covered by Big Ideas, and that Honors Algebra 1 is a "completely different experience" than the high school course; a majority wanted Math 6/7 and Math 7/8 offered again. Middle School D teachers called IM "a good choice, but not perfect," noted reading level as a barrier, reported parent requests for at-home practice and a textbook, and asked to separate 8th grade content from Algebra 1 via a 6/7 and 7/8 track.

THROUGHLINES. Affirmation of IM as Tier 1 curriculum, with the view that it needs additional resources and that it is too soon to walk away; vertical alignment from 5th to 8th grade; an accelerated pathway beginning in grade 6 given the wide range of skills in Math 6 and Math 7; different ways to provide Math 8 content prior to Algebra 1 and alignment of the middle school Algebra 1 course to the full-year high school offering; a practice resource aligned to IM units plus a parent resource for at-home support; and review of scheduling and PD for more consistent grade-level collaboration.

GOALS, LEARNING, AND CELEBRATIONS. Goals of the 2023 change: improve Tier 1 instruction for all; align instruction to district vision; students as do-ers of math; task-based mathematics; fluency through conceptual understanding; increased access to high levels of math and honors math; and transparency in opportunities for all students. Lessons learned: some families do not feel heard or valued; the shift to task-based instruction is a substantial change; teachers need ongoing support and collaboration; families need more concrete materials at home; students need more skills and fluency practice outside of story problems. Celebrations: a higher percentage of students are enrolled in honors/accelerated math in 8th and 9th grade today than before 2024 (the first year of choice); consistent MSTEP improvement over the last three years, specifically increases in the advanced performance band and reductions in the not proficient band in 7th grade; and 93% of middle school students report they feel they can be good at math.

RECOMMENDED NEXT STEPS. (1) Create an Honors Alg 1 work group beginning summer 2026 to address content overload in Honors Alg 1/Math 8, exploring summer learning modules, designing a fall assessment for student feedback, communicating with families, and continuing through the 26/27 school year. (2) Create or purchase resources for at-home learning and support in summer 2026, identifying a resource for at-home practice and assessments aligned with IM units and implemented across buildings, and creating a parent resource bank in a common location. (3) Vertical alignment beginning summer 2026 through a work group on 5th grade and 6th grade learning targets. (4) Pilot Accelerated Math 6/7 for fall 2026, beginning spring 2026, with cohorts of Math 6 and Math 6/7 teachers beginning training, materials for parents developed the week of 5/4, 5th grade (incoming 6th grade) parent nights the week of 5/4, a maintained test-out structure for Math 6, and an opt-in structure for Accelerated 6/7 by parent choice. (5) Ongoing 26/27 work to identify "on ramps" and "off ramps" for all students, develop resources, establish grade-level cohorts, affirm pilot implementation and next steps for grades 7 and 8, and make a recommendation to the Board in early spring (March/April 2027).

After reviewing rubrics from The Reading League, EdReports and ESSA, visiting 14 curriculum vendors and four districts, the review committee scored Collaborative Literacy at 96% among K-5 comprehensive options and UFLI at 88% among K-5 foundational skills options, both of which move to pilot; grades 6-8 will pilot two finalists, Arts & Letters (47%) and EL Education (41%), with a board recommendation planned for April 2027.

**What it is**
A Troy School District presentation to the Board of Education dated April 28, 2026, titled "K-8 Literacy Curriculum Review Update." It frames the work around the science of reading and structured literacy, reports the review committee's process and scoring, and lays out the pilot and adoption timeline.

**PA 146 components and process**
The overview lists the components of PA 146: assessments, multi-tiered systems of support, literacy coaching, professional learning, English learners, and suggested Tier 1 elementary reading curricula, together with the Troy K-8 Tier 1 pilot process update and the MDE timeline. The district's review process began with a Curriculum Review Committee composed of classroom teachers, literacy specialists, ELD specialists, special education teachers, principals and district administrators, Teaching and Learning staff, and the Literacy Leadership Team.

**Research and data review**
Data reviewed included aggregate national, state, county and district trends (including the NAEP Reading Assessment), TSD subgroup data, and perception data from staff, families and students. K-5 staff reported a positive view of responsive teaching, small group instruction, intervention, book clubs and a high-engagement curriculum with choice and voice, and recommended more explicit phonics and vocabulary instruction. K-5 families were positive about their child's literacy growth, confidence and book bags/book clubs, and asked for stronger emphasis on phonics, spelling and decoding plus more take-home materials. Grades 6-8 staff valued student choice with novels and peer-to-peer dialogue and wanted more whole-class novels, assessment-supporting materials and scaffolding; families valued choice, book clubs and high-interest materials and wanted grammar, spelling and vocabulary instruction.

**Shared learning**
Oakland Schools supports included the PA 146 Leadership Series, Instructional Leadership Network, MTSS Handbook, and sessions on structured literacy and the reading brain including students with dyslexia, plus ongoing consultant work on the adoption process. MDE provided a LETRS training cohort. The team completed vendor visits with 14 curriculum vendors, some multiple times, and district visits to Novi and Birmingham (Arts and Letters), South Lyon (Collaborative Classroom and UFLI), and West Bloomfield (EL Education). Research highlights cited Nell Duke, Mark Seidenberg, Robert J. Tierney and P. David Pearson, Timothy Shanahan, and Katherine Marsh in The Atlantic.

**Rubrics and scoring**
MDE rubrics were applied in three phases: Phase 1 The Reading League, Phase 2 EdReports, Phase 3 ESSA, alongside TSD rubrics aligned to the district vision and pillars. Pillar averages used a 2-Strong, 1-Moderate, 0-Weak scale.

| Band / category | Option | Result |
|---|---|---|
| K-5 comprehensive | Collaborative Literacy | 96% |
| K-5 comprehensive | HMH Into Reading | 4% |
| K-5 comprehensive | Arts and Letters / EL Education / SAVVAS / CKLA | 0% |
| K-5 foundational | UFLI | 88% |
| K-5 foundational | 95 Phonics Core | 8% |
| K-5 foundational | Magnetic Reading | 4% |
| K-5 foundational | Really Great Reading / Reading Horizons | 0% |
| 6-8 | Arts & Letters | 47% |
| 6-8 | EL Education | 41% |
| 6-8 | HMH Into Literature | 6% |
| 6-8 | Amplify | 6% |
| 6-8 | SAVVAS | 0% |

**Pilots**
K-5 pilots are designed to inform implementation at scale: a Collaborative Literacy pilot with a "35m allocation," and a UFLI pilot. The 6-8 pilot is designed to inform selection between two options, Arts & Letters and EL Education. Arts & Letters is described as grounded in cognitive science with 60-minute lessons, customizable slide decks and organized notes; EL Education is described around mastery of knowledge and skills, character, and high-quality student work.

**Timeline**
May 11 Community Night; August 2026 collaboration with vendors; October 2026 collaboration with vendors; November through March pilots and ongoing support; April 2027 board recommendation.

The process stages presented are Research and Vision, then Explore and Pilot.

DATA REVIEW. The research and vision phase included a data review across three categories: aggregate data covering national, state, county and district trends; subgroup data covering TSD's current subgroups; and perception data from staff, families and students. National and statewide trends were presented using the NAEP Reading Assessment.

PERCEPTION DATA, K-5. K-5 staff expressed a positive view of opportunities for responsive teaching, small group instruction, intervention, book clubs, and a high engagement curriculum offering choice and voice, and recommended more explicit instruction in phonics and vocabulary. K-5 families expressed a positive view of their child's literacy growth, the confidence their child shows in literacy skills, and book bags/book clubs, and recommended a stronger emphasis on phonics, spelling and decoding skills along with more materials sent home for parents to use with students.

PERCEPTION DATA, 6-8. Grades 6-8 staff expressed a positive view of student choice with novels and peer-to-peer dialogue about in-class texts, and a desire for more whole class novels, materials that support assessment, and more scaffolding of tasks. Families expressed a positive view of student choice in what they read, book clubs, and high interest materials, and a desire for instruction in grammar, spelling and vocabulary. A student feedback section is also included.

SHARED LEARNING. Through Oakland Schools the team participated in the PA 146 Leadership Series, the Instructional Leadership Network, the MTSS Handbook, "Structured Literacy & the Essential Practices: What, Why, and for Whom?" and "The Reading Brain: Implications for All, Including Students with Dyslexia," plus ongoing consultant work with Oakland Schools around the curriculum adoption process. Through MDE the district participated in a LETRS training cohort. Vendor visits covered 14 curriculum vendors, some multiple times. District visits were made to Novi and Birmingham for Arts and Letters, South Lyon for Collaborative Classroom and UFLI, and West Bloomfield for EL Education.

RESEARCH HIGHLIGHTS. Shared readings included "The Science of Reading Progresses: Communicating Advances Beyond the Simple View of Reading" by Nell Duke; "Structured Literacy and the Science of Reading" by Mark Seidenberg; "Fact Checking the Science of Reading" by Robert J. Tierney and P. David Pearson; Timothy Shanahan's piece on what role, if any, phonics should play in middle school or high school; and "Why Kids Aren't Falling in Love with Reading" by Katherine Marsh in The Atlantic. Learning shared with all PK-12 teachers and administrators covered reading models (balanced literacy and structured literacy), the pilot process, and pilot feedback.

K-8 LITERACY VISION. The stated vision holds that literacy learning is a complex, purposeful process integrating reading, writing, speaking and listening, aiming to develop joyful, engaged and lifelong readers and writers through authentic learning experiences that balance explicit instruction with student choice and voice. The district commits to a cohesive K-8 literacy framework that values high-volume reading, strong foundational skills, and differentiated instruction, and to ensuring curriculum and practices reflect students' identities, cultures and language development needs. It commits to centering students in decision-making, honoring teacher expertise, and continuous improvement through research, collaboration and effective professional learning, valuing authenticity, access, equity and rigor, and preparing students with the literacy skills, stamina and critical thinking needed for college, career and life.

RUBRICS. MDE rubrics were used in three phases: Phase 1, The Reading League; Phase 2, EdReports; Phase 3, ESSA (Every Student Succeeds Act). TSD rubrics were applied in alignment with the district's vision and pillars. Pillar averages were reported on a scale of 2-Strong, 1-Moderate, 0-Weak.

K-5 COMPREHENSIVE CURRICULUM RESULTS. Reviewed options and results: Collaborative Literacy 96%; HMH Into Reading 4%; Arts and Letters 0%; EL Education 0%; SAVVAS 0%; CKLA 0%. Collaborative Literacy is described as a comprehensive, evidence-based K-5 program intentionally integrating foundational skills, deep comprehension and rich knowledge-building literacy experiences with daily social skills instruction. On alignment with evidence-based practices, The Reading League indicated that Collaborative Literacy effectively incorporates critical components of Scarborough's Reading Rope including background knowledge, vocabulary, language structures, verbal reasoning and literacy knowledge. Word recognition components include letter recognition, handwriting, word study, spelling instruction, phonics and phonological awareness; language comprehension components include metacognitive strategies for navigating genres and text types plus explicit vocabulary, structure and word study instruction. Assessment features include placement and progress monitoring tools, embedded formative assessments, and end-of-unit summative assessments measuring growth across comprehension, vocabulary, word study and spelling. Differentiated instruction features whole class instruction, targeted small group placement-based foundational skills instruction, daily independent practice, supports for MLL learners and reteach units. Texts include interactive read alouds, trade books and decodables, IDR libraries, book clubs, and nonfiction articles supporting knowledge building.

K-5 FOUNDATIONAL SKILLS RESULTS. Reviewed options and results: UFLI 88%; 95 Phonics Core 8%; Magnetic Reading 4%; Really Great Reading 0%; Reading Horizons 0%. UFLI is described as an explicit and systematic program following a carefully developed scope and sequence so students systematically acquire each skill and apply it with automaticity and confidence. Targeted skills include phoneme blending and segmenting practice; accuracy and automaticity of grapheme-phoneme correspondences; decoding automaticity of words with previously learned concepts; explicit introduction of new concepts; decoding and encoding practice; reading and spelling irregular words; reading and spelling connected text; and supplemental decodable passages with optional homework practice.

K-5 PILOTS. Framed as piloting to inform implementation at scale, the K-5 plan includes a Collaborative Literacy pilot with a "35m allocation" and a UFLI pilot.

GRADES 6-8 RESULTS. Reviewed options and results: Arts & Letters 47%; EL Education 41%; HMH Into Literature 6%; Amplify 6%; SAVVAS 0%. Arts & Letters is described as developed with cognitive science and learning sciences research guiding instructional design, with a lesson structure creating optimal cognitive conditions for learning; its comprehension features include consistent models for collaboration, an integrated approach to writing, reading and language development, instructional routines, and a focus on building knowledge; engagement features include high quality materials, flexible support and meeting the needs of varied learners; usability features include 60-minute lessons, clear instructions, customizable slide decks, and organized notes for efficient and dynamic teaching. EL Education is described as expanding the definition of student achievement to honor students' full humanity, drawing on decades of research on social, emotional and academic development, organized around mastery of knowledge and skills (apply learning, think critically, communicate clearly), character (become effective learners, become ethical people, contribute to a better world), and high quality student work (create complex work, demonstrate craftsmanship, create authentic work).

GRADES 6-8 PILOTS AND K-8 COHESION. The 6-8 pilot is framed as piloting to inform selection between two options, Arts & Letters and EL Education. K-8 cohesion criteria are that materials excite educators, connect to the district's vision and values, teach the Michigan Standards, and align to PA 146 and the science of reading.

NEXT STEPS WITH TIER 1 MATERIALS. May 11, community night; August 2026, collaboration with vendors; October 2026, collaboration with vendors; November through March, pilots and ongoing support; April 2027, board recommendation.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Memorandum from MJ School Policy Services (Miller Johnson) to policy service clients, dated March 9, 2026, transmitting the March 2026 policy manual and administrative regulations update in the Troy School District board packet. It contains nine numbered updates, 22.01 through 22.09, with no recommended changes to the Introduction, Bylaws or Personnel series. The most consequential item is Update 22.03, revising Policy 2006 to comply with MCL 380.1303a as amended by House Bill 4141 and Senate Bill 495, signed February 10, 2026, which requires boards to prohibit student use of wireless communication devices during instructional time effective in the 2026-27 school year.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What it is**
A memorandum from MJ School Policy Services to MJ Policy Service Clients, dated March 9, 2026, subject "Policy Manual and Administrative Regulations Update - March 2026." Revisions are presented by section with an individual update number, additions shown in red, deletions in blue, and yellow highlighting where the district must supply additional information. Questions are directed to Policy@MillerJohnson.com. Eleven margin comments (DT1 through DT11) carry the firm's accept/decline recommendations.

**Sections with no recommended updates**
Introduction (0000 Series), Bylaws (1000 Series), and Personnel (4000 Series).

**Students - 2000 Series**
Update 22.01, Policy 2003 Education Records: the fiscal year 2026 State School Aid Act adds MCL 388.1764k requirements for districts and ISDs regarding student surveys. Parents may inspect all materials used for any student survey, analysis or evaluation connected to a program funded by the U.S. Department of Education, and consent is required before a student participates in one revealing political or religious affiliations, mental or psychological problems, sexual behavior or attitudes, illegal or self-incriminating behavior, critical appraisals of close family relations, privileged relationships such as lawyers, physicians and ministers, or income. Questions and results of district-wide, state or federally mandated, and grade-level-wide surveys must be posted on the district website with parent notification, subject to FERPA.

Update 22.02, Policy 2004 Extracurricular Activities: applies to MHSAA member districts. The MHSAA approved an expansion of its personal branding activities (PBA)/name, image, or likeness (NIL) rule, Regulation I, Section 11 C - Amateur Status/Awards, on January 23, 2026, effective immediately. The policy prohibits PBA/NIL agreements that violate Board Policy or the Student Code of Conduct and bars PBA/NIL activity during school hours or events or on district property without prior written approval from the Superintendent.

Update 22.03, Policy 2006 Behavior: House Bill 4141 and Senate Bill 495 were signed by Governor Whitmer on February 10, 2026, amending MCL 380.1303a to require a board policy prohibiting wireless communication device use during instructional time for the 2026-27 school year. Definitions cover wireless communication devices, instructional time and school grounds; devices must be turned off and out of sight in lockers or cubbies. Exemptions cover medically necessary devices, district-owned or issued devices, instructional use at staff discretion, special education programming or accommodations under a Section 504 Plan, IEP or the ADA, lesson-specific assignments, and emergency situations under the district's Emergency Operations Plan pursuant to MCL 380.1308b. Recording or broadcasting others requires permission, except at activities where personal recording is generally permitted.

**Curriculum and Instruction - 3000 Series**
Update 22.04, Policy 3003 Instruction: under MCL 388.1764k, the district must notify parents by September 30, 2026 if it uses a K-5 curriculum not on the state's evidence-based list per MCL 380.1280f.

**Remaining series**
Update 22.05, Policy 5003 Purchasing: corrects a spelling error, replacing "statuses" with "statutes." Update 22.06, Policy 6013 Facility Dog: clarifies that facility dogs are School District owned dogs trained to work in school facilities and at events. Update 22.07, Policy 7001 Goal: adds record retention language tied to the Michigan Department of Technology, Management & Budget retention schedule for school districts, with disposal permitted after the retention period absent a litigation hold. Update 22.08, Policy 7008 Advertising: bars advertising on district-owned property without the Superintendent's written consent and directs regulations on accepting commercial advertisements. Update 22.09, Policy 8003 Website and Digital Content Accessibility: conforms the policy to WCAG 2.1 Level AA per updated U.S. Department of Justice requirements, with periodic accessibility audits of the website, online platforms and mobile applications.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Memorandum from MJ School Policy Services, the school policy practice of Miller Johnson, to MJ Policy Service Clients, dated March 9, 2026, subject "Policy Manual and Administrative Regulations Update - March 2026," included in the Troy Board of Education packet. The memo states that proposed revisions are presented by section with a specific update number for ease of reference (for example, Update 22.01), that additions to policy or administrative regulation language are shown in red and deletions in blue, and that areas highlighted in yellow require additional information from the district to complete the update. Because each district's manual is unique and modified consistent with district priority and prerogative, some recommended modifications may already appear in completed manuals; questions are directed to Policy@MillerJohnson.com, and districts behind on updates are invited to contact the office for compliance support. Eleven margin comments, labeled Commented [DT1] through Commented [DT11], record the firm's recommendation on each change.

SECTIONS WITH NO RECOMMENDED UPDATES. The Introduction (0000 Series), Bylaws (1000 Series), and Personnel (4000 Series) sections each carry the note that there are no recommended policy updates for the section.

UPDATE 22.01 - POLICY 2003, EDUCATION RECORDS (STUDENTS, 2000 SERIES). The fiscal year 2026 State School Aid Act includes MCL 388.1764k, which imposes additional requirements on school districts and intermediate school districts regarding student surveys. Adoption is recommended to ensure compliance with Section 164k, with reference to Miller Johnson guidance titled "New Compliance Requirements Under Section 164k - State School Aid Act (FY 2025-2026)" and "Additional Guidance on Section 164k Compliance - District Surveys & Curriculum Requirements." The redlined policy provides that parents may inspect all materials used for any student survey, analysis, or evaluation conducted by the School District in connection with a program funded by the United States Department of Education, and that the district will not, without parental consent, require a student to participate in one that reveals or is intended to reveal information concerning the student or the student's parents' political or religious affiliations, beliefs or practices; mental or psychological problems; sexual behavior or attitudes; illegal, anti-social, self-incriminating or demeaning behavior; critical appraisals of other individuals with whom the student or parents have close family relationships; legally recognized privileged or analogous relationships, such as those with lawyers, physicians and ministers; or income, other than when required by law to determine eligibility for programs or financial assistance. In compliance with MCL 388.1764k, the district will ensure that questions and results of district-wide surveys, state or federally mandated surveys, and surveys distributed to all students in a grade level are made available to the public by posting on the district's website, with parents notified, while complying with the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) before releasing any survey results. Comments DT1 and DT2 recommend accepting the added mandatory MCL 388.1764k language.

UPDATE 22.02 - POLICY 2004, EXTRACURRICULAR ACTIVITIES. This update applies to districts that are members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA). The MHSAA approved an expansion of its personal branding activities (PBA)/name, image, or likeness (NIL) rule - Regulation I, Section 11 C - Amateur Status/Awards on January 23, 2026. Effective immediately, a student may earn compensation through personal branding activities, such as promoting or endorsing a product or service, regardless of whether the activity relates to athletics. The policy provides that the Superintendent, in consultation with the Board and selected district personnel, will develop and administer a robust program of interscholastic athletics adhering to the principle that participants are students first and athletes second. In addition to MHSAA regulations, the district prohibits students from engaging in PBA/NIL agreements that violate Board Policy or the Student Code of Conduct, with discipline available for violations, and provides that PBA/NIL activities shall not occur during school hours or events or on School District property unless prior written approval is provided by the Superintendent. Comment DT3 recommends accepting the proposed changes to ensure students still comply with Board Policy and the Student Code of Conduct.

UPDATE 22.03 - POLICY 2006, BEHAVIOR. Governor Whitmer signed House Bill 4141 and Senate Bill 495 on February 10, 2026. Collectively they amend the Revised School Code, specifically MCL 380.1303a, to require a board of education to adopt a policy prohibiting students from using a wireless communications device during instructional time, effective for the 2026-27 school year. Referenced guidance is titled "New Law Prohibits Students from Using Wireless Communication Devices - Effective 2026-2027 School Year." The redline replaces the term "personal electronic devices" with "wireless communication devices" and defines a wireless communication device as an electronic device capable of, but not limited to, text messaging, voice communication, entertainment, navigation, accessing the internet, sending and receiving photos and videos, or producing email. "Instructional time" means time that any student is assigned to engage in learning and curricular activities by instructional staff. "School grounds" means a building, playing field, or property used for school purposes to impart instruction to students or used for functions and events sponsored by a school. Under the prohibition, in accordance with MCL 380.1303a, students are prohibited from using wireless communication devices on school grounds during instructional time and the school day unless required by law; the prohibition will be enforced by instructional staff through monitoring students during instructional time and the school day; and devices must be turned off and kept out of sight in lockers or cubbies. Exemptions permit use of a wireless communication device during instructional time and the school day for medically necessary devices; district owned or issued devices under building staff discretion; devices used for instructional purposes with building staff discretion; devices used for special education programming and/or as an accommodation under a Section 504 Plan, Individualized Education Program, or the Americans with Disabilities Act; devices used for lesson-specific academic assignments at building staff's discretion; and devices used in emergency situations as described in the district's Emergency Operations Plan, where applicable per the plan, pursuant to MCL 380.1308b. On recording and broadcast, students may not use wireless communication devices to broadcast or record audio, images or video of any student, staff member or other person in the school or while attending a school-related activity without permission from the person to be recorded; this does not apply to curricular or extracurricular activities for which personal recording is generally permitted, such as athletic events and arts performances. The Superintendent may develop administrative regulations consistent with the policy. Comments DT4 and DT5 recommend accepting the proposed changes to ensure compliance with MCL 380.1303a.

UPDATE 22.04 - POLICY 3003, INSTRUCTION (CURRICULUM AND INSTRUCTION, 3000 SERIES). The fiscal year 2026 State School Aid Act includes MCL 388.1764k, adding requirements for districts and intermediate school districts when an evidence-based curriculum for grades K-5 is not used, per MCL 380.1280f. The policy provides that, to the extent feasible, student instruction will be delivered using research based and peer reviewed instructional methodologies, and that in compliance with MCL 388.1764k the district will notify parents by September 30, 2026 if it uses a curriculum not on the state's evidence-based list for grades K-5. The Superintendent may develop consistent regulations. Comment DT6 recommends accepting the proposed changes for compliance.

UPDATE 22.05 - POLICY 5003, PURCHASING (BUSINESS, 5000 SERIES). A correction of a minor spelling/grammatical error. The policy provides that the Superintendent will promulgate legally-compliant administrative regulations concerning expenditures of funds received through state and federal grants and awards, and shall establish and maintain effective internal control over financial grants and awards providing reasonable assurance that the program and funds are managed in compliance with applicable statutes (replacing "statuses"), regulations, and the terms and conditions of the awards. Comment DT7 recommends accepting the correction.

UPDATE 22.06 - POLICY 6013, FACILITY DOG (FACILITIES AND OPERATIONS, 6000 SERIES). This update clarifies the definition of a "facility dog" and states the policy should be used for school district owned dogs. Facility dogs are School District owned dogs trained to work within school facilities and at school events with children with a variety of academic, social and emotional needs, and the Superintendent will promulgate an administrative regulation applicable to the use of facility dogs on district property. Comment DT8 describes it as a minor wording adjustment to be made with the establishment of a Facility Dog policy.

UPDATE 22.07 - POLICY 7001, GOAL (SCHOOL AND COMMUNITY RELATIONS, 7000 SERIES). An additional section addressing record retention: the district will retain all public records in accordance with the Michigan Department of Technology, Management & Budget retention schedule for school districts, and unless the district is in receipt of a litigation hold or similar notice, records may be disposed of after the retention period in accordance with the state schedule. Comment DT9 notes the addition further addresses record retention policies.

UPDATE 22.08 - POLICY 7008, ADVERTISING. The revision gives districts more flexibility in preparing regulations regarding accepting advertisements generally. No advertising may be distributed, posted or displayed on or within any District-owned property without the written consent of the Superintendent, and the Superintendent shall prepare regulations addressing the circumstances under which the district would consider accepting advertisements, including but not limited to commercial advertisements. Comment DT10 recommends accepting the minor language adjustment.

UPDATE 22.09 - POLICY 8003, WEBSITE AND DIGITAL CONTENT ACCESSIBILITY (GENERAL POLICIES, 8000 SERIES). The revisions ensure compliance with the WCAG 2.1 Level AA standard per recently updated requirements of the U.S. Department of Justice, with reference to Miller Johnson guidance "New ADA Rules for District Websites & Apps." The policy commits the district to ensuring its website, online platforms and mobile applications are accessible to students, parents, employees and members of the public; all pages on the district's website, online platforms and mobile applications will conform to the W3C WAI Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, Level AA conformance, or any updated equivalent standard; the district will continue to evaluate and test future releases and updates and remains committed to serving the widest possible audience; and to support this commitment the district will conduct periodic accessibility audits of its website, online platforms and mobile applications. Comment DT11 describes it as a compliance adjustment to policy.

**What it is**
Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education for Tuesday, March 17, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, submitted by Secretary Matt Haupt (MH/jh) and carried in the April 21, 2026 packet.

**Attendance**
President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present with Mrs. Anne were board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Recker, Montante, Pagel and Trudel, plus approximately 75 audience members. The meeting adjourned at 8:24 p.m.

**Recognition**
Michigan School Band and Orchestra Association All-State students were honored, introduced by orchestra teacher Mrs. Claire Murphy. Selection typically involves around 2,500 students competing for about 400 seats, with blind adjudication, a three-day rehearsal schedule, and a culminating performance at DeVos Performance Hall during the Michigan Music Conference in Grand Rapids. Students from Adam Burns' Athens class presented "Why Native Plants?", a documentary short produced for an environmental journalism grant from the Knight Center for Journalism at Michigan State University. CURRICULUM. None.

BUSINESS - ENROLLMENT PROJECTIONS REPORT. Mr. Trudel shared the report on the annual enrollment projections provided by Plante Moran and explained that the Board reviewed it in detail at the March 7th Board Retreat with Plante Moran representatives. **Autism Acceptance Month resolution**

Its recitals state that Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States; that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report that 1 in 36 children may have autism; that autism is a neurological and developmental disorder characterized by social impairment and restricted interactive and communication behaviors that can affect anyone regardless of race, ethnicity, gender or socioeconomic background; that symptoms may present in a variety of combinations and can result in significant, lifelong challenges affecting learning, daily living, employment, social-interactive behaviors, and understanding verbal and nonverbal communications; that physicians, psychologists, behavior analysts, speech and language pathologists, occupational therapists, vocational rehabilitation professionals and educators can assist persons with autism and their families through early identification, education, intervention and recreation; and that the Troy School District is committed to fostering acceptance and belonging. **Business Services, item a: Easement Agreement**

**Business Services, item b: Declaration of necessity and condemnation authorization**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic. The Board declared it necessary to acquire permanent highway easements and sidewalk easements along Livernois Road for the new Smith Middle School project, noting that negotiations with the Owner had not been successful and that the District has power to acquire interests in real property by condemnation under the Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act.

Key elements of the resolution:

Special board meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education for Tuesday, April 7, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. **Business Services, item a: Easement Agreement**
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt, the Board resolved to authorize the Sidewalk Easement and Highway Easement and to authorize the Superintendent of the School District, or his designee, to execute the Sidewalk Easement and Highway Easement as well as any and all documents necessary and incidental on behalf of the School District.

The recitals state that the Troy School District desires to grant a Sidewalk Easement and a Highway Easement to the Board of County Road Commissioners of the County of Oakland in order to construct, install, operate, use, maintain, repair, replace and remove a sidewalk and roadway for the new Smith Middle School on each Property (collectively the Properties), in accordance with the terms of the Sidewalk Easement and the Highway Easement; and that the School District desires to authorize the Superintendent, or his designee, to execute those easements on terms substantially similar to those in the attached documents, which are attached and incorporated by reference as Exhibit A.

The operative provisions are: (1) the School District authorizes the Sidewalk Easement and Highway Easement on terms substantially similar to those contained in the attached instruments; and (2) the Superintendent of the School District, or his designee, is authorized to execute the Sidewalk Easement and Highway Easement as well as any and all documents necessary and incidental on behalf of the School District.

A certification block headed RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED follows, certifying that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a resolution duly adopted by the Board of Education of Troy School District, County of Oakland, Michigan, at a special meeting held on the 7th day of April, 2026, and that the meeting was conducted and public notice given pursuant to and in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, being Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, and that minutes were kept and will be or have been made available as required by that Act. The certification is signed by the Secretary, Board of Education. The recorded vote is Yes: 7, No: 0.

**Business Services, item b: Declaring necessity to acquire highway and sidewalk easement and authorizing legal counsel to initiate condemnation proceedings for the Smith Middle School project**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic. The resolution states that negotiations with the Owner to acquire the easements have not been successful; that the District has power to acquire interests in real property by condemnation pursuant to the Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act; and that the Board finds it necessary to acquire permanent highway easements and sidewalk easements along Livernois Road.

The recitals identify the Troy School District as a Michigan general powers school district acting by and through its Board of Education, currently undertaking a project for construction and operation of the new Smith Middle School (the Project) located on Livernois Road in the City of Troy, Oakland County, Michigan, which includes roadway and sidewalk improvements necessary for the benefit of the public and to improve road conditions, safety, mobility and accessibility to the school and for road users. As part of the Project it is necessary to construct driveway approaches and a deceleration lane on the east side of Livernois Road, including widening the road and making traffic signal and sidewalk improvements, collectively the Livernois Road Improvements.

To undertake the Project the District must acquire permanent highway and sidewalk easements on, over, across and under certain real property owned in fee by Mirza Azam-Ali Baig and Juveria Baig, husband and wife (the Owner), situated in the City of Troy, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, commonly known as 5836 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan, Tax Parcel No. 20-10-101-033. The Easements are set forth in the Declaration of Necessity and Taking of Property attached in substantial form as Exhibit A.

Statutory authority cited includes Section 11a of Michigan Public Act 451, Public Acts of 1976 (The Revised School Code), as amended, MCL 380.11a, under which the District has power to acquire interests in real property by condemnation, and the Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act, Public Act 87 of 1980, as amended, MCL 213.51 et seq. (the UCPA), which establishes procedures for the taking of property by eminent domain. The District reserves the right to bring federal or state cost recovery actions against the Owner for costs incurred as a result of the release of hazardous or toxic substances or materials that may have occurred on the Easement. The District will present the Owner a good faith written offer to acquire the Easement in exchange for payment of just compensation based on an appraisal by a state certified appraiser; if the Owner rejects that offer, the Clark Hill PLC law firm is authorized to institute a condemnation lawsuit for acquisition of the Easements, and the Superintendent of Schools or the Deputy Superintendent of Schools of Business Affairs is authorized to execute any documents needed for the condemnation lawsuit.

The operative provisions are numbered 1 through 6. (1) The Board declares that the Project is a public improvement and that acquiring the Easements in, on, over, under, across and through the Property for the Livernois Road Improvements is necessary and essential, since those improvements benefit the public and improve public safety. (2) The Board authorizes the Superintendent of Schools, or in his absence the Deputy Superintendent of Business Affairs, to take all action and execute documents necessary under the Revised School Code, the UCPA and any other applicable state or federal law, including acquiring the Easements, recording the Statement of Necessity and Declaration of Taking of Private Property in substantial form as set forth in Exhibit A, retaining qualified appraisers or other consultants to determine just compensation, making good faith written offers to property owners, entering negotiations, reaching agreements as to just compensation, presenting good faith offers to Owners and interested parties, and initiating appropriate proceedings in the Oakland County Circuit Court for condemnation of the Easements set forth in Exhibit A. (3) The Deputy Superintendent of Schools of Business Affairs is authorized to establish an escrow account with First American Title Company for the specific amounts estimated to be just compensation for the Easements to be condemned pursuant to the UCPA. (4) Clark Hill PLC, or in the event of conflict such other firm as the Superintendent may select, is retained to take all appropriate action regarding initiation of condemnation proceedings in the Oakland County Circuit Court for the taking of private property as indicated in Exhibit A. (5) The Deputy Superintendent of Schools of Business Affairs is authorized to select a real estate appraiser or other consultants, considering estimated appraisal cost, timing of services, professional services and expert witness qualifications, to prepare estimates of just compensation required for the Easement taken as described in Exhibit A. (6) The Board of Education for the Troy School District reserves the right to bring federal or state cost recovery actions against the Owner for costs incurred as a result of the release of hazardous or toxic substances or materials that may have occurred on the Easement.

**Other: rescheduling of the Board Workshop**
Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Potts, the Board resolved to reschedule the May 5, 2026 Board of Education Workshop to the preceding week, April 28, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. No separate vote tally is printed in the minutes for this item or for Business Services item b; the only recorded tally in the minutes is Yes: 7, No: 0 on the Easement Agreement.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Titled "Board Narrative Summary — Special Education Budget Reductions, Proposed Reduction Scenario" and dated June 2026, the paper explains to the Troy School District Board of Education how the proposed special education reductions were developed and how those specific reductions connect to the broader budget plan presented to the Board. It opens by stating that special education remains one of the district's highest priorities and one of its largest areas of investment.

SCORING METHOD AND TIER DEFINITIONS
The proposals were produced through the district's structured scoring process. Each was evaluated across six weighted criteria: impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support. Weighted scores then determined tier placement. Tier 1 is defined as a strong candidate, scoring 4.0–5.0; Tier 2 as "consider," scoring 3.0–3.9; Tier 3 as high risk, requiring further study, scoring below 3.0. The summary states that savings figures reflect actual FTE and actual dollar savings as entered in the scoring matrix.

WHY SPECIAL EDUCATION IS PART OF THE CONVERSATION
The narrative attributes the inclusion of special education in the reduction scenario to six years of cost growth that is described as no longer sustainable within the district's structural budget. Between 2018–2019 and 2024–2025, special education costs rose 74% — an increase of more than $12.4 million — while the number of students served grew by only 3%. The accompanying comparison table reports Special Education Costs (IEP and non-IEP) of $16,744,610 in 2018–2019 and $29,210,999 in 2024–2025, a change of +$12,466,389 (74%); and Special Education Student Count of 1,332 in 2018–2019 and 1,367 in 2024–2025, a change of +35 (3%). The gap between cost growth and enrollment growth is identified as the central reason special education is included in the scenario.

A second driver is a state-led shift in how certain special education services are delivered. Several of the proposals align district staffing to new county-level service plans and county targets. Taken together, the reductions are described as intended to right-size staffing to current requirements while preserving the services students are entitled to.

COMMITMENTS TO STUDENTS
The summary states that the district's core obligations to students with disabilities do not change. All special education programs will continue to be staffed in alignment with state and county requirements, including certified teachers, paraprofessionals, and related service providers. Decisions are guided by each student's Individualized Education Program (IEP) and are mandated to comply with all legal and educational standards. As the district adapts to the state-led shift in service delivery, it will continue to provide services based on IEP needs and state requirements while making responsible adjustments to ensure the long-term sustainability of its programs.

SUMMARY OF PROPOSED REDUCTIONS
The proposed reductions fall into two categories, classroom instruction and non-instructional supports. Special Education – Classroom Instruction comprises 4 proposals with annual savings of $1,396,573 and a tier mix of 2 Tier 1 / 1 Tier 2 / 1 Tier 3. Special Education – Non-Instructional comprises 4 proposals with annual savings of $1,833,312 and a tier mix of 2 / 2 / 0. Total Special Education Reductions are stated as 8 proposals, $3,229,885 in annual savings, with a tier mix of 4 / 3 / 1.

CLASSROOM INSTRUCTION REDUCTIONS — $1,396,573
These proposals adjust instructional special education staffing to align with new county-level service plans and county staffing targets. Three of the four are described as strong or consider-level candidates; one — the adjustment of Teacher Consultant and Resource Room (TC/RR) staff to county targets — carries the highest risk in the special education set and is flagged for further Board discussion. The itemized proposals are:
• Adjust TC/RR staff to meet county targets (3.7 Elementary, 3.6 Secondary) — annual savings $635,100, weighted score 2.95, Tier 3, status "Flag for review."
• Teacher reduction based on new county level plan (3 L4, 1 ECP) — annual savings $348,000, score 4.10, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Paraprofessional reduction based on new county level plan — annual savings $236,270, score 4.10, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Elementary Resource Room paraprofessionals reduction — annual savings $177,203, score 3.85, Tier 2, status "Consider."
The subtotal for the category is $1,396,573. The narrative repeats that the TC/RR adjustment is the only Tier 3 proposal in the special education set, with a weighted score of 2.95, and that per the scoring framework it warrants further study before adoption.

NON-INSTRUCTIONAL REDUCTIONS — $1,833,312
These proposals reduce non-instructional support staffing. The largest single special education reduction in the entire scenario sits in this category: the reduction of general education Student Support Aides from 158 to 104 FTE, which the narrative says accounts for more than $1.3 million in savings. The remaining proposals adjust social worker, psychologist, and clerical staffing. The itemized proposals are:
• Student Support Aide – Gen Ed (from 158 to 104 FTE) — annual savings $1,334,362, score 4.15, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Social Workers reduction (from 24.4 to 21.4 FTE) — annual savings $348,000, score 3.90, Tier 2, status "Consider."
• Psychologist reduction (from 10 to 9 FTE) — annual savings $116,000, score 3.90, Tier 2, status "Consider."
• Special Education Secretary — annual savings $34,951, score 4.35, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
The subtotal for the category is $1,833,312. The narrative notes that the social worker and psychologist reductions are Tier 2 (consider) proposals and may benefit from phased implementation.

RISK AND PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS
Of the eight special education proposals, four are Tier 1 (recommended), three are Tier 2 (consider, with additional planning), and one is Tier 3 (high risk). In practical terms, the narrative states that the four Tier 1 proposals — totaling roughly $1.95 million — are strong candidates with low risk and high feasibility and are recommended for inclusion; that the three Tier 2 proposals — the Elementary Resource Room paraprofessional, social worker, and psychologist reductions — may be included with additional planning, communication, or phased implementation; and that the single Tier 3 proposal, the TC/RR staffing adjustment to county targets, is flagged for further Board conversation before it is adopted. It adds that proposals scoring below 4.0 may still be included if savings are critical to meeting the reduction goal, but that they require additional planning, communication, and mitigation efforts.

HOW THE REDUCTIONS FIT THE OVERALL PLAN
Because special education is governed by IEPs and by state and county requirements, the proposals were scored with particular attention to legal and compliance risk and to equity impact. The stated intent is to bring staffing back into alignment with current service requirements and the state-led delivery model — not to reduce services students are entitled to receive — while contributing meaningfully toward closing the structural budget gap.

Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education for Tuesday, June 16, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:18 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members Alic, Melton, Potts, and Zendler were present; Mr. Haupt and Dr. Philippart were absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Moran, Anderson, Montante, Pagel, and Trudel. Approximately 50 members of the audience attended. The meeting opened with the Pledge of Allegiance and adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

PUBLIC HEARING: 2026/2027 PROPOSED BUDGET
Mr. Trudel shared an overview of the 2025-2026 final budget amendments as well as the 2026-2027 budget proposals. His presentation addressed taxable values, the Headlee amendment, homestead millage comparisons, general fund versus ancillary funds, the capital project fund, the common debt fund, the sinking fund, the capital maintenance fund, special revenue funds, the food service fund, the Troy Career Center fund, the community service fund, the Troy Preschool fund, and the student activities fund.

RECOGNITION: RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF GUN SAFETY AND SAFE GUN STORAGE
Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses state that the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and staff is a top priority in the Troy School District; that firearms are now the leading cause of death among U.S. children and adolescents due to rising rates of homicide, suicide, and unintentional shootings, compounded by social inequities, increased access to guns, and insufficient safety measures; that rates of death from firearms among ages 14 to 17 are higher than motor vehicle-related death rates, and that middle and high school age children in the U.S. are now more likely to die as the result of a firearm injury than from any other single cause of death; that according to a report from the US Secret Service, in incidents of gun violence on school grounds 76% of attackers acquired a firearm from the home of a parent or another close relative; that since 2025 there have been over 240 unintentional shootings by children, resulting in 39 deaths and 72 injuries nationally; that more than 28,000 Americans are estimated to have died by suicide using firearms in 2025; that research indicates close to 5 million US children live in a home with a loaded and unlocked firearm; that evidence strongly suggests secure firearm storage is an essential component of any effective strategy to keep the community safe; that keeping students, teachers, and staff safe from the threat of gun violence should be the responsibility of all adult stakeholders within the school district; and that preventative measures require action now.

The resolved clauses direct the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm safety and violence prevention measures during gun violence awareness month, and to disseminate material on an annual basis stressing the importance of secure storage of firearms by including it in the district's annual notification materials; commit the Board and Superintendent to continue working with local law enforcement agencies, medical and mental health agencies, and non-profit organizations to inform district parents of their obligations regarding secure storage of firearms in their homes as well as other gun violence prevention safety measures; and state that the resolution shall not be construed to conflict with any existing Michigan or federal law. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Haupt and Philippart absent; the resolution was declared adopted. A certification by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Board of Education, attests that the resolution was duly adopted at a regular meeting held on the 16th day of June, 2026, conducted with public notice given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, being Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

RESOLUTION URGING PASSAGE OF THE 2026/2027 SCHOOL AID BUDGET BY JULY 1ST
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Zendler. The whereas clauses note that with only two weeks remaining in the fiscal year for schools the Legislature had not yet passed a School Aid Budget; that last year the budget was not passed until after the Constitutional October 1 deadline, forcing districts to make critical staffing and programming decisions based on speculation rather than certainty, and that without a budget schools cannot responsibly plan for staffing, class sizes, transportation, or essential services; that Troy School District is legally obligated to complete its budget by the end of June and will fulfill that obligation, but without certainty from Lansing will again be forced to consider freezing programs, delaying hires, and laying off staff; that the framework for a responsible School Aid fund budget already exists within the three proposals under consideration; that focus should remain on passing a responsible, balanced budget rather than beginning discussions on major reforms, with significant property tax changes or other structural changes deserving thorough debate separate from the budget; and that policymakers must complete a School Aid budget including an inflationary increase to the foundation allowance, weighted funding for at-risk and ELL students, an end to the diversion of K12 dollars away from the classroom, and a fix to school safety and mental health funding. The resolved clauses call on the Legislature and the Governor to pass the School Aid Budget before July 1 and direct that a copy be forwarded to the district's representatives in the Michigan House of Representatives and the Michigan Senate as well as the Governor's office. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Haupt and Philippart absent; the motion was declared adopted, certified by Matt Haupt, Secretary.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS / PUBLIC COMMUNICATION
Additions and deletions: none. During public communication on agenda items, five community members addressed the Board; no action was taken. Public communication on non-agenda items: none. Personnel: none. Curriculum: none. Other: none.

GENERAL – CONSENT AGENDA
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Melton that the Board approve items A through J on the consent agenda: minutes of the May 19, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report – April 2026; Food Service Contract Renewal; Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) Membership – 2026/2027; 2025/2026 Budget Amendment; 2026/2027 Budget Appropriations Resolution; Common Debt Fund Resolution; approval of OCSBA Association Bylaws Amendment; approval of an OCSBA new resolution opposing tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege; and AP Precalculus Textbook Adoption. The vote was Yes 4 – Alic, Anne, Melton, Zendler; No 1 – Potts; Absent Haupt and Philippart.

BUSINESS ITEMS
MacBook/iPad Purchases: moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mrs. Alic that the district purchase Apple MacBooks and iPads in the amount of $2,420,430.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart.
Bus Purchase: moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Melton that the bid for school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $2,464,089.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart.

BOARD COMMENTS
Listed comments included encouraging the community to reach out to legislators to pass the budget on time; thanks to speakers who spoke during public comment, with the note that the board hears them; congratulations to the Class of 2026 graduates; Men's Mental Health Awareness Month; appreciation for secretaries; Board members requesting a special meeting to discuss budget reductions further; counselor ratios and special education positions; the August 4th ballot countywide millage, under which $780 per student would come from the Enhancement Millage, just under $9,000,000 to Troy School District; a comment that the public education landscape is not good; and Happy Father's Day and Juneteenth celebration.

ADJOURNMENT AND NEXT MEETING
