https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A letter dated June 15, 2026 from Matt Jansen, Troy School District Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, asks the MHSAA Executive Board to waive the cooperative team enrollment limitation so Troy High School and Troy Athens High School may form a combined "Troy United" boys lacrosse program beginning in 2026-27. The two schools' combined enrollment of 3,936 students exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements. The request is framed by a projected $12.1 million district budget deficit and by declining participation, with only 41 players projected to return across the two programs before incoming freshmen.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Document**
Letter dated June 15, 2026 to the Members of the MHSAA Executive Board, on Troy School District District Athletics letterhead — Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., Superintendent of Schools; Matt Jansen, Director, Athletics; 1522 E. Big Beaver Rd., Troy, Michigan 48083; 248.823.5154, fax 248.823.5133. Signed by Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment.

**Request**
Approval of a waiver to the current cooperative team enrollment limitation to allow Troy High School and Troy Athens High School to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program beginning with the 2026-27 school year, operating as a single "Troy United" program.

**Enrollment**

| School | Enrollment |
| --- | --- |
| Troy High School | 2,127 |
| Troy Athens High School | 1,809 |
| Combined | 3,936 |

The combined figure exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements, which is why a waiver is sought.

**Financial context**
The district is facing a projected $12.1 million budget deficit entering the 2026-27 school year. As part of district-wide reductions, the Athletics Department has been tasked with reducing expenditures by approximately $100,000. The district recently discontinued financial support for non-MHSAA sanctioned sports, including synchronized swimming and boys and girls water polo; those programs moved to self-funded club status, generating approximately $50,000 in annual savings. A cooperative boys lacrosse program would provide an estimated annual savings of approximately $25,000.

**Participation**

| Measure | Troy High School | Troy Athens High School |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026 season participants | 48 | 31 |
| Graduating seniors | 21 | 13 |
| Projected returning participants | 26 | 15 |

Combined returning participation is stated as 41 players before the addition of incoming freshmen. Of the 15 projected returners at Athens, only one participated at the varsity level during the 2026 season; the remaining 14 had never played lacrosse prior to 2026. Athens attempted to field both varsity and junior varsity teams but could not consistently maintain enough healthy student-athletes to sustain junior varsity competition through the season.

**Program stability**
Following the 2026 season, the Troy Athens varsity boys lacrosse coach informed the district of his decision to step down, citing as a significant factor the ongoing difficulty of building and sustaining a program with limited participation. Troy Athens has historically participated in a cooperative arrangement with Avondale Schools, which in recent years has yielded no more than two players annually and contributed no participants during the 2026 season; the letter concludes that partnership is no longer viable.

**Precedent cited**
Within the Oakland Activities Association and surrounding communities: Farmington and North Farmington; Royal Oak and Berkley; Birmingham Groves and Birmingham Seaholm; Waterford Mott and Waterford Kettering; Milford and Lakeland; the Livonia Public Schools combined program; South Lyon's combined program; Bishop Foley and Clawson; Brandon and Holly; the St. Clair Shores cooperative program; and Eisenhower and Utica.

**Position**
The letter states the request is not intended to create a competitive advantage but to preserve participation opportunities, maintain both varsity and junior varsity levels of competition, and sustain access to boys lacrosse. It notes the proposal has the full support and approval of Troy School District administration, including the Superintendent, Assistant Superintendent, both high school principals, and the Athletic Department.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Correspondence dated June 15, 2026, addressed to the Members of the MHSAA Executive Board, sent on Troy School District District Athletics letterhead listing Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., Superintendent of Schools, and Matt Jansen, Director, Athletics, at 1522 E. Big Beaver Rd., Troy, Michigan 48083, telephone 248.823.5154, fax 248.823.5133. The letter is signed by Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, and carries the footer "An Equal Opportunity/Affirmative Action Employer."

THE REQUEST
On behalf of the Troy School District, the letter requests approval of a waiver to the current cooperative team enrollment limitation to allow Troy High School and Troy Athens High School to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program beginning with the 2026-27 school year. The combined enrollment of the two high schools is 3,936 students, with Troy High School enrolling 2,127 students and Troy Athens High School enrolling 1,809 students. The letter acknowledges that this total exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements but argues that the circumstances warrant special consideration and approval.

FINANCIAL CONTEXT
The Troy School District is described as currently facing a projected $12.1 million budget deficit entering the 2026-27 school year. As part of district-wide reductions, the Athletics Department has been tasked with reducing expenditures by approximately $100,000. To address these financial challenges, the district recently discontinued financial support for non-MHSAA sanctioned sports, including synchronized swimming and boys and girls water polo. Those programs have transitioned to self-funded club status, generating approximately $50,000 in annual savings. The letter calls this a difficult decision and states that additional measures are necessary to maintain sustainable athletic opportunities for students. A cooperative boys lacrosse program between Troy High School and Troy Athens High School would provide an estimated annual savings of approximately $25,000 while preserving participation opportunities for student-athletes at both schools.

PARTICIPATION AND PROGRAM SUSTAINABILITY
The letter emphasizes that the request is driven more by participation numbers and program sustainability than solely by financial considerations. During the 2026 boys lacrosse season, Troy High School had 48 participants while Troy Athens High School had 31 participants. Troy High School is graduating 21 seniors and Troy Athens High School is graduating 13 seniors. This leaves projected returning participation numbers of only 26 student-athletes at Troy High School and 15 student-athletes at Troy Athens High School, for a combined total of 41 returning players before the addition of incoming freshmen.

The situation at Troy Athens is described as particularly concerning. Of the 15 projected returning players, only one participated at the varsity level during the 2026 season; the remaining 14 players had never played lacrosse prior to the 2026 season. Although Athens attempted to field both varsity and junior varsity teams in the spring, the program was unable to consistently maintain enough healthy student-athletes to sustain junior varsity competition throughout the season.

COACHING AND PRIOR COOPERATIVE ARRANGEMENT
These challenges are said to have affected program leadership and long-term stability. Following the 2026 season, the Troy Athens varsity boys lacrosse coach informed the district of his decision to step down, with a significant factor being the ongoing difficulty of building and sustaining a program with limited participation numbers. The letter presents this as further illustration of the challenges facing the Athens program and the need for a more sustainable model. Historically, Troy Athens has participated in a cooperative arrangement with Avondale Schools, but that partnership has not provided the participation numbers necessary to sustain the program: in recent years the cooperative agreement has yielded no more than two players annually, and during the 2026 season Avondale contributed no participants. The letter concludes that the Avondale partnership is no longer a viable long-term solution.

RATIONALE FOR A COMBINED PROGRAM
The letter states that one of the fundamental goals of interscholastic athletics is to provide meaningful participation and developmental opportunities for as many student-athletes as possible. A cooperative program would allow the district to maintain both varsity and junior varsity competition, ensuring that beginning and developing players have an appropriate environment in which to learn, improve, and remain engaged in the sport; without sufficient numbers to sustain a junior varsity program, opportunities for skill development and long-term participation are significantly diminished. Establishing a single "Troy United" boys lacrosse program is presented as a stable structure that supports program numbers while preserving access and opportunity for student-athletes from both schools, aligning with the educational mission of the MHSAA by prioritizing participation, student development, and the long-term viability of boys lacrosse within the community.

REGIONAL PRECEDENT
The letter argues the request is consistent with cooperative programs that already exist throughout the region. Within the Oakland Activities Association and surrounding communities, numerous school districts have been permitted to combine programs to preserve participation opportunities. Examples cited include Farmington and North Farmington, Royal Oak and Berkley, Birmingham Groves and Birmingham Seaholm, and Waterford Mott and Waterford Kettering. Additional area examples cited are Milford and Lakeland, the Livonia Public Schools combined program, South Lyon's combined program, Bishop Foley and Clawson, Brandon and Holly, the St. Clair Shores cooperative program, and Eisenhower and Utica. The Troy School District states it is simply seeking the same opportunity to preserve a viable boys lacrosse program for its students.

CLOSING POSITION AND APPROVALS
Approval of the waiver would allow the district to establish a single "Troy United" boys lacrosse program representing both Troy High School and Troy Athens High School, providing the participation numbers necessary to maintain both varsity and junior varsity opportunities while supporting the district's ongoing financial sustainability efforts. The letter states the request is not intended to create a competitive advantage but rather to preserve participation opportunities, maintain both levels of competition, and ensure that student-athletes in the Troy School District continue to have access to boys lacrosse in a sustainable and educationally sound manner. The proposal is reported to have already received the full support and approval of the Troy School District administration, including the Superintendent, the Assistant Superintendent, both high school principals, and the Athletic Department. The letter closes by respectfully requesting that the Executive Board grant the waiver to the cooperative enrollment limitation and approve the cooperative boys lacrosse program, thanking the board for its consideration and offering to provide any additional information the Council may require.

**Purpose and Process**
The High School Course Description Book (CDB) shows the course requirements and elective opportunities available to Troy School District students and is organized by department so that students and families understand the offerings. It is a OneTroy document developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools along with the Teaching and Learning team. The CDB is updated annually as part of the district's curriculum review process; each year department teams determine where course descriptions should be updated to reflect new curriculum and instruction, and where courses should be added or deleted. The changes described here apply to the 2026/2027 school year.

**Courses Added**

| Course | Grades | Length / Credit | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AP Business with Personal Finance | 9-12 | Full Year, 1.0 credit | Satisfies 1 credit of math-related graduation requirement; students meet the introductory requirement to compete in DECA the following year |
| AP Cybersecurity | 9-12 | Full Year, 1.0 credit | Replaces and builds upon the previously offered Cybersecurity course; part of AP Career Kickstart |
| AP Precalculus AB | 9-12 | Full Year, 1.0 Credit | Requires Algebra 2; replaces the previously offered Precalculus; prepares students for AP Calculus AB |
| AP Precalculus BC | 9-12 | Full Year, 1.0 Credit | Requires Algebra 2; replaces the previously offered Honors Precalculus; adds limits, derivatives, and vectors; prepares students for AP Calculus BC |
| Career Capstone | 11-12 | 1 Semester, 1/2 credit | Requires completer status in a business pathway (Finance, BAMO, or Marketing) |
| Mathematics of Tabletop Games | 11-12 | 1 Semester, 0.5 Credit | Requires Geometry; satisfies 0.5 credit of math-related graduation requirement |
| Sports Officiating | 9-12 | 1 Semester, 0.5 Credit | Students become certified high school officials upon course completion |

**English 11 Semester Choices**
English 11 Semester 1 is titled "Literary Analysis in Reading; Writing about Reading," with students choosing one of three half-credit Grade 11 options: Great American Stories (texts may include The Great Gatsby, A Raisin in the Sun, Fences), Contemporary American Literature (texts may include Kindred, King James, Sweat), and American Dramas and Musicals (texts may include Hamilton, View from the Bridge, King James). English 11 Semester 2 is titled "Writing with a Purpose and Exploring Mentor Texts," again with a choice of one half-credit course: Persuasive Writing, Writing Imaginative Fiction, or Writing Personal Memoirs. All three Semester 1 courses include focused sessions on preparing for the SAT; all three Semester 2 courses include focused sessions on writing a rhetorical essay in response to the SAT prompts and creating a working draft of a personal essay. Writing Imaginative Fiction prepares students to take Creative Writing 2 in senior year.

**Courses Removed**
The removals are described as offerings that have not run in the past five years.

**Other Changes**
Achievement Skills III will now be called Integrated Studies III. The district reports increased math-related and NCAA course approvals. The CDB format is changed from PDF to PaperTurn.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Curriculum item presented to the Troy School District Board of Education for its January 20, 2026 meeting, documenting the annual revision of the High School Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2026/2027 school year.

**Nature and governance of the CDB.** The High School Course Description Book shows the course requirements and elective opportunities for students, organized by department so that students and families understand the offerings. The CDB is a OneTroy document, developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools along with the Teaching and Learning team, and updated annually as part of the district's curriculum review process. Each year, department teams determine where course descriptions should be updated to reflect new curriculum and instruction, as well as where courses should be added or deleted. The changes enumerated below were made for the 2026/2027 School Year.

**Courses Added**

*AP Business with Personal Finance* — Grades 9-12, Full Year, 1.0 credit. The course satisfies 1 credit of the math-related graduation requirement. It introduces students to the knowledge and skills they will need to grow their careers, manage money, and get a head start toward the most popular college major in the U.S. Developed in partnership with college faculty and industry leaders, the yearlong course offers the opportunity to earn college credit and an employer-endorsed credential. Participants meet the introductory requirement to have the potential to compete in DECA the following year.

*AP Cybersecurity* — Grades 9-12, Full year, 1.0 credit. A yearlong high school course offering a broad introduction to the field and aligning closely with a college-level introductory cybersecurity course. It replaces and builds upon the previously offered Cybersecurity course. Students learn about common threats and vulnerabilities and how they combine to create risk; study how individuals and organizations manage risk and how risk can be mitigated through a defense-in-depth strategy; and explore vulnerabilities, attacks, mitigations, and detection measures across domains including physical spaces, computer networks, devices, and data and applications. Students consider the impact of cybersecurity on individuals, organizations, societies, and governments. Content and skills align with the professional skills outlined in the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education Workforce Framework. AP Cybersecurity is part of the AP Career Kickstart group of courses, designed to accelerate high school students on their paths to in-demand careers, and offers the opportunity to earn an employer-endorsed credential in the cybersecurity field.

*AP Precalculus AB* — Grades 9-12, Full Year, 1.0 Credit. Students must have completed Algebra 2 to be enrolled. AP Precalculus is a college-level mathematics course preparing students for advanced study in calculus and other STEM fields, and it replaces the previously offered Precalculus. Through the study of functions, modeling, and problem-solving, students develop understanding of the concepts underlying calculus. Major topics include polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions; polar and parametric equations; and the analysis of rates of change. Students may take the AP Precalculus exam and are prepared to take AP Calculus AB.

*AP Precalculus BC* — Grades 9-12, Full Year, 1.0 Credit. Students must have completed Algebra 2 to be enrolled. AP Precalculus BC is a college-level mathematics course preparing students for advanced study in calculus and other STEM fields, and it replaces the previously offered Honors Precalculus. It covers the same major topics — polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions; polar and parametric equations; and the analysis of rates of change — with the additional content of limits and derivatives and vectors. Students may take the AP Precalculus exam and are prepared to take AP Calculus BC.

*Career Capstone* — Grades 11-12, 1 Semester, 1/2 credit. Students must be a completer in a business pathway (Finance, BAMO, or Marketing) to be enrolled. Described in the text as the CTE Professional Capstone, it is a culminating experience designed to prepare students for college, careers, and real-world professional environments. Students build a professional identity by developing a resume, LinkedIn profile, and digital portfolio showcasing their CTE work, engage in professional-based learning projects that mirror authentic industry challenges, and collaborate with business partners to design solutions. Employability skills are refined through formal interview practice, career coaching, job-shadow opportunities, and reflective activities. Students graduate with a professional toolkit supporting future job applications, internships, apprenticeships, and postsecondary pathways.

**English 11 — Semester 1: Literary Analysis in Reading; Writing about Reading (Students Choose 1).** Each option is Grade 11, 1 Semester, 0.5 Credit.

*English 11 1 - Great American Stories* introduces students to influential and enduring works of American literature. Through short stories, novels, dramas, and historical texts, students explore themes such as identity, freedom, justice, the American Dream, and societal change. Texts may include classic works such as The Great Gatsby, A Raisin in the Sun, Fences, and/or other timeless works. The course emphasizes critical reading, textual analysis, historical context, and writing, and includes focused sessions on preparing for the SAT.

*English 11 1 - Contemporary American Literature* examines the contemporary landscape of American literature, focusing on how contemporary writers grapple with the promises and contradictions embedded in the American experience. Through novels, short stories, poetry, essays, and plays, students explore themes such as freedom, equality, justice, identity, race, immigration, and belonging. Texts may include contemporary works such as Kindred, King James, Sweat, and/or other present-day publications. The course emphasizes critical reading, textual analysis, historical context, and writing, and includes focused sessions on preparing for the SAT.

*English 11 1 - American Dramas and Musicals* introduces students to dramas by American playwrights about the American Dream, American identity, and how the American experience is reflected in the plays of the 20th and 21st century. Students also interact with musicals that explore identity and self-invention through music and performance while learning about the traditions of the American musical form. Texts may include dramas such as Hamilton, View from the Bridge, King James, and/or other plays and musicals. The course emphasizes critical thinking about dramas and musicals, analysis of character and theme, historical context, and writing about drama, and includes focused sessions on preparing for the SAT.

**English 11 — Semester 2: Writing with a Purpose and Exploring Mentor Texts (Students Choose 1).** Each option is Grade 11, 1 Semester, 0.5 Credit.

*English 11 2 - Persuasive Writing* is a semester-long course designed to empower students to think critically, argue effectively, and communicate with clarity and confidence. Through reading, writing, speaking, and listening experiences, students learn to craft logical, evidence-based arguments and transform them into oral presentations. Students explore real-world issues, analyze model texts, and study rhetorical techniques used by accomplished speakers, practicing forming claims, selecting strong evidence, addressing counterarguments, and adapting their message to diverse audiences. The course includes focused sessions on writing a rhetorical essay in response to the SAT prompts and creating a working draft of a personal essay.

*English 11 2 - Writing Imaginative Fiction* invites 11th grade students to explore the art of imaginative writing. Students develop their creative voices while learning essential elements of storytelling — character, setting, plot, dialogue, and narrative structure — as well as poetic techniques such as imagery, metaphor, rhythm, and form. Through reading influential authors and poets, engaging in writing workshops, and experimenting with a variety of styles, students expand their understanding of how language can inspire emotion, spark ideas, and communicate complex experiences. The course prepares students to take Creative Writing 2 in senior year and includes focused sessions on writing a rhetorical essay in response to the SAT prompts and creating a working draft of a personal essay.

*English 11 2 - Writing Personal Memoirs* invites 11th grade students to explore memoir writing as a way to discover and shape their voices as authors. Through close reading of mentor texts — memoirs, personal essays, and narrative nonfiction — students study how writers transform lived experiences into stories that connect with readers, learning narrative techniques such as sensory detail, structure, reflection, and the use of voice to reveal identity and perspective. Guided workshops encourage students to write from personal experience and experiment with form and tone. Each student produces a polished memoir and a collection of shorter writings. The course includes focused sessions on writing a rhetorical essay in response to the SAT prompts and creating a working draft of a personal essay.

**Additional new courses.**

*Mathematics of Tabletop Games* — Grades 11-12, 1 Semester, 0.5 Credit. The course qualifies as a 1/2 math-related credit, and students must have completed Geometry to be enrolled. Students collaboratively investigate the mathematical foundation of various tabletop games through theorycrafting, experiential observation, and empirical analysis, forging a connection between combinatorics, geometry, probability, game theory, and logic and the medium of tabletop games. The course satisfies 0.5 credit of the math-related graduation requirement.

*Sports Officiating* — Grades 9-12, 1 Semester, 0.5 Credit. Students learn to officiate sports and become certified high school officials upon course completion. The course covers three sports per semester: football, basketball, and a sport of students' choice in the Fall semester; baseball, softball, and soccer in the Spring semester, along with a sport of students' choice. It is designed to help students work competently and comfortably as an official immediately upon completion, and students earn referrals to local recreational leagues, middle schools, and sub-varsity scholastic assignors.

**Courses Removed.** The item states that none of these offerings has run in the past five years. Social Studies: Political Science; Stories of Yourself and Others; Psychology 2; Conflicts of the 20th Century; Philosophy. English: Literature of Suspense; Science Fiction; Voices in Literature; Modern Shakespeare. Life Skills: Interior Design; Stitchery.

**Other Changes.** Achievement Skills III will now be called Integrated Studies III. The district notes increased math-related and NCAA course approvals. The format of the Course Description Book is changed from PDF to PaperTurn.
